pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 8: Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 8, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren’t about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit’s point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

1. Kevin Huerter

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons’ rotation this season. In a game where Detroit’s entire backcourt didn’t really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he’d be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he’s hitting 40% from deep this season.

2. John Collins and Paul Reed

Detroit’s starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain’t pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it’s the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it’s two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It’s an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers’ big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion’s share of the blame goes to Collins. He’s been quite bad all season, and it’s getting less clear by the day how he’s going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don’t think he’s ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn’t surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

3. Austin Reaves

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he’d never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

4. Daniss Jenkins

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, “This is not going to happen.”

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He’s got scoring in his blood, and he’s more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard’s body. He’s got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he’s better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he’s not running the offense.

4. The refs.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs Lakers preview: Best Defense vs best offense
pistons.body:
Does it get any better than the No. 1 offense versus the No. 1 defense? The Detroit Pistons find themselves in that matchup as the 122-point-per-game Los Angeles Lakers visit Motown tonight.

Luka Dončić and the Lakers put up plenty of buckets, but scoring on Detroit is still an impossible task. The Pistons only surrender 101 points a game. Smothering defense every night.

Detroit’s defense has its biggest test of the season if Dončić suits up this evening. He’s questionable with lower back tightness.

It would be a shame if we’re robbed of Cade Cunningham going head-to-head with another MVP candidate. The bigger shame would be if we miss out on Dončić versus Ausar Thompson. That matchup is like Jerry Rice versus Deion Sanders with how both are operating.

GAME VITALS

Where: Little Caesars Arena, Detroit, MI

When: 6 PM EST

Watch: TV20 Detroit/DAZN-DET

Odds: Pistons (-4.5)

Analysis

Detroit hasn’t played since Wednesday’s loss to the Philadelphia 76ers. They’ve had plenty of time to rest up. They’ll need it if Dončić suits up.

Dončić is averaging 40 points. He’s shooting 42% on nearly 14 3s a game. He gets to the line more than anybody. It’s basically no stopping Dončić at the moment. This is a Wilt Chamberlain-like hot streak. Those two are the only players to average 40 nine games into the season. Whew, to say he’s balling is an understatement.

But tasks like this are why the Pistons employ Ausar Thompson. If *anybody* can slow Dončić down, it’s the best perimeter defender on the planet. Dončić usually has success against quick defenders with wiry strength, but Ausar is bigger and stronger this season. We’ll be keeping tabs on how Ausar takes Dončić’s bumps tonight. Ausar has the quick hands to disrupt things as well.

This might be a game where we see Paul Reed getting to the level and blitzing a bunch. J.B. Bickerstaff may decide to get the ball out of Dončić’s hands and force someone else to beat them. Reed is capable of coming to the level on screens and muddying things up.

I’m sure Dončić will see some Cade tonight too. Cade won’t make it easy with his sturdy frame. On the other end, the Lakers only have a few perimeter defenders to throw at Cade.

Matisse Thybulle is firmly in LA’s rotation as he’s started all 10 games. He’s still a defensive playmaking threat. Cade deals with defenders like this nightly, but Thybulle is a plus defender nonetheless. So is Ziaire Williams. The springy 25-year-old treats every possession as if he’ll never get in the game again if he doesn’t go hard.

Those two are solid defensively, and Jake LaRavia competes. Outside of that, Detroit will have plenty of favorable matchups (Walker Kessler is a great rim protector and is off to a good offensive start. He can make a difference).

Dončić displays effort and is trying to shake the terrible defender narrative on his name, but attacking him is still the best way to slow him down. Make him work and keep him involved in actions.

Austin Reaves falls into the same boat. He’s under Dončić on the Lakers’ best defenders on the team list. Anybody with that matchup should look to be aggressive.

Reaves spends most of his time covering shooting guards. Will JJ Redick make Reaves chase Duncan Robinson all night? That’s probably not ideal. Robinson runs even great defenders into the ground.

Robinson’s light-em-up stretch continues as he’s fourth in 3s made (35). Only Dončić, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Steph Curry have made more.

Detroit is letting it fly from deep as a team. According to Cleaning the Glass, 40 percent of their shots are coming from 3 (15th) compared to 31 percent last year (29th). Their rim rate has flipped the other way, but getting Jalen Duren back should rectify that.

The best offense versus the best defense is a mandatory viewing appointment. Can Ausar slow down the MVP-favorite? Do the Pistons show why they’re an elite defense and smother Dončić as a team? Does Cade deliver a masterclass against a guy he’ll be compared to for the foreseeable future if he’s in the MVP race? We’ll find out at 6 PM. Be there!

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (6-2): Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

Los Angeles Lakers (8-2): Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia, Walker Kessler

Question of the day

What are your thoughts on Austin Reaves? He reportedly did not want to be drafted by Detroit. Does that still bother you?

pistons.headline: The Pistons go from owning to getting owned in the paint
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Jalen Duren #0 of the Detroit Pistons looks on from the bench during a game against the Philadelphia 76ers at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

During a tumultuous playoff run and a prolonged offseason contract negotiation, Detroit Pistons fans were ready to say goodbye to Jalen Duren. Well, Duren has been out for six of eight games, and it turns out that Duren is the most indispensable member of the Pistons aside from Cade Cunningham.

A hamstring strain has knocked Duren out for six straight and counting, and boy, do you feel that every moment of every Pistons game.

Pundits and fans alike had easy diagnoses for what ailed the 60-win team during a disappointing second-round exit last season. Detroit needed a second scorer and much more perimeter shooting to succeed in the postseason. Its second-best player, the All-NBA big man Duren, couldn’t effectively operate in a congested, constipated offense when opponents had so much extra time to prepare their defense. That had a trickle-down effect on Cade Cunningham and on offensively limited players the Pistons relied on, like Ausar Thompson, Javonte Green, and Ron Holland.

This offseason, the Pistons seemingly tried and failed to add their second scorer (a planned run at Austin Reaves fizzled, and trade interest in players such as Kyrie Irving and Kevin Durant went nowhere). But they certainly addressed the team’s lack of perimeter punch. Detroit added guys such as Isaiah Joe, John Collins, and Taurean Prince. They re-signed midseason acquisition Kevin Huerter. They reformulated their offensive game plan to create more movement, space, and offensive responsibility among their non-Cade players. So far this season, the perimeter offense has hummed. Detroit is a top-10 team in 3-point shooting and almost middle of the pack in attempts despite Isaiah Joe missing most of the season to injury.

Detroit is 6-2, losing to the New York Knicks and on Wednesday night to the East-leading Philadelphia 76ers. Calls after both games from fans and casual watchers immediately turn to the team’s lack of that second star as the biggest issue. While that still might be a deal-breaker in the players, I would argue that the actual biggest issue in the season’s first eight games is Detroit’s collapse in its former ability to absolutely own the paint.

In other words, it’s not the lack of a Kyrie or a Durant or a Devin Booker. It’s the lack of Duren.

Last season, Detroit led the NBA in points in the paint, mostly behind Duren’s elite rim gravity and chemistry with Cade Cunningham and Detroit’s other ball handlers. Last season, the Pistons led the NBA with 57.9 points in the paint and were fourth in opponents’ paint scoring. They had a scoring differential inside of 14.2 points per game.  This season, Detroit ranks just 22nd in the paint at 44.8, down 13.1 points per game.

Rim gravity, it turns out, is just as important as perimeter shooting in creating the space needed to run a successful offense.

Paul Reed is a dynamic scorer inside, and he has some pop to his game. But he isn’t a rim runner like Duren. You give it to him on the block, and you let him work his magic. John Collins is opportunistic in transition, but those opportunities are dried up when he is the only big on the floor applying rim pressure, usually trying to duck in from the corners.

Ausar has the ball in his hands more, and it is working to create opportunities from others on the perimeter, but it is taking away a lot of those dunker-spot opportunities and back cuts that Thompson feasted on last season.

The lack of inside pressure is manifesting in other ways. Detroit has gone from a top-5 team in second-chance points to 22nd. They are 28th in offensive rebounding. Last season, they were third.

This team needs Jalen Duren back ASAP. And I think fans need to start reckoning with how crucial he is for this team to succeed.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers final score: Detroit falls short in East battle
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons drives around Vj Edgecombe #77 of the Philadelphia 76ers during the first half at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons (6-2) fall short in the battle between the top teams in the Eastern Conference. The Philadelphia 76ers (8-1) outlasted Detroit 112-106. Philly got up by as many as 18 points, but Detroit never truly went away. The 76ers’ stardom showed its head tonight.

After holding Jaylen Brown to 16 points in the first meeting of the season, he surpassed that in the first half this time around. Brown poured in 30 points for the game while converting on 11 of his 19 shots. He rained in spot-up 3s, as it was tough to stick with him with the way Philly forced Detroit into scramble mode throughout the ballgame. Brown had a clutch block on Cade, and his presence was felt on both sides of the ball.

This is not 2023 Joel Embiid, but he’s still a force. Embiid still draws double teams and can get any big in foul trouble. He and Tolu Smith got into a dust-up that injected some life into Detroit, but Philly found a way to withstand every Detroit storm.

Duncan Robinson went on a few personal runs that seemed to turn the tide in Detroit’s favor. The sharpshooter went for 27 points and buried an unconscious seven triples. Robinson’s ability to look past the hands in his face to shoot the rock will pay dividends all season. It didn’t work out tonight, but Robinson is off to a different type of start as a sniper.

Cade Cunningham tried to put on his cape and emptied the clip. He couldn’t find it from deep but got good looks. He went for 26 points, 11 assists, and seven boards. He got to the charity stripe and nailed every attempt (7-7). Cade had another LeBron-like chasedown block — this time in LeBron’s presence.

At this point, those are truly Cade-like chasedowns, and Brown’s missed layup here shows Cade’s reputation as a chasedown artist is evident.

Jaylen Brown misses the wide open layup. 😬 pic.twitter.com/jMyfS41RJG
— Hoop Central (@TheHoopCentral) November 5, 2026

VJ Edgecombe had a fast break sequence where he u-turned it because Cade was on the hunt again. Special defender.

Ausar Thompson’s special stuff came on the boards as he snagged 17 rebounds tonight. From the opening possession, he was pogo-sticking down low to help Paul Reed and John Collins in the paint. AT chipped in 11 points, and his shot from the line continues to look better. He was 3-for-4 tonight; you’ll take the small improvements wherever you can.

John Collins had his best offensive game in a few games. He was getting behind the defense, throwing down head-top slams. His ability to be a paint finisher and hit threes is why he’s here. He only shot one 3 tonight. The Pistons need more.

Collins should look better when Duren comes back, in theory. Duren has rim-gravity that forces defenses to account for one of the best finishers in basketball. This was the first game where I thought Detroit missed Duren badly. From a talent perspective, Detroit was outgunned tonight.

LeBron James controlled the tempo in spurts of the game. He was playing like that OG at the Y who’s keeping up with the youngins on pure know-how. LeBron draws two to the ball, Embiid does, Brown does, and Tyrese Maxey does. There’s a lot of star power over there, and this is a team Detroit could see in the long run.

The Pistons did not have their sharpest defensive night, and Philly still only cracked 112. It was just one of the games. Detroit shifts their focus to another superstar in Luka Dončić. He and the Los Angeles Lakers travel to Detroit on Sunday as the Pistons take on their first Western Conference team of the season.

One benefit in Detroit’s favor is that this is a nationally televised game on ESPN, and it seems like Cade Cunningham loves to come up big when the lights are brightest for national television. pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers preview:  East’s top two teams square off on National TV
pistons.body:
If you are to believe preseason predictions, this game being a showdown between the East’s top two teams could come as a bit of a surprise.  Pistons fans knew this team would be good, but many talking heads predicted a falloff this season while everybody was on board with the 76ers being one of the best teams in the league.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that the team that was 1st in the East last season is once again competing for the top seed in the East, but talking heads have to make their money somehow.  ESPN at least had the foresight to pickup this game and you get what should be a very fun early-season showdown between two teams that have only lost one game each.

The 76ers and Pistons have played once this season and the Pistons won, but it is tough to draw any conclusions since both teams were missing a couple of starters.

Game Vitals

Where:  Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, MI
When:  Wednesday, November 4 at 7 pm EST
Watch:  ESPN
Odds:  Detroit (-2.5)

Analysis

The Pistons will be without Jalen Duren and Isaiah Joe, who was already ruled out for this game last night.  The Pistons were missing Jalen Duren in the last matchup between these teams and also Ausar Thompson, who they will have back.  But, Isaiah Joe did suffer the hip injury that is still keeping him out during the 1st quarter of the last matchup, so the Pistons are trading one injured player for another.

With this being a National TV game and the 76ers getting a day of rest, I would suspect that everybody plays for them tonight.  In the last matchup, the 76ers did not have Joel Embiid or VJ Edgecombe, which really put their lack of depth to the test.

Joel Embiid’s size and ability on the glass could become a problem for the Pistons, who will continue to start the undersized Paul Reed and likely use John Collins to back him up.  Without Jalen Duren, rebounding was already going to be a problem, but the Pistons have been able to overcome it during his absence.

In the last matchup, the Pistons were able to contain Tyrese Maxey through 3 quarters before he started hitting shots in the 4th.  It was a bit of shocking development since the Pistons were without Ausar Thompson, but without some of the other stars for the 76ers, they could focus their defense more on stopping Maxey.  The 76ers have a lot of star power, but their biggest offensive threat is arguably Maxey, who can hit shots from anywhere on the court and can use his quickness with the ball to get to where he wants.  I would expect Ausar Thompson to draw the Tyrese Maxey matchup which will allow Cade Cunningham to guard Jaylen Brown since he has the size to keep up with him.

Paul Reed is outsized by him and also can have some issues with fouling and Joel Embiid has made a living off of bating fouls throughout his career.  Paul Reed is going to have to stay disciplined, as I don’t think the Pistons can afford to have heavy minutes of John Collins at center or Tolu Smith.  I have full confidence in the Pistons’ ability to matchup with the rest of the 76ers starting lineup, but the most concern I have is this matchup and it very well could swing the game.

If there is one certainty for the Pistons, it is that Cade Cunningham is difficult to slow down, especially with how he is playing now.  He is coming off a 33 points masterclass against the Charlotte Hornets on Monday in only 27 minutes where he absolutely took over the game and turned a single-digit lead into a 20-plus point blowout.  Cade Cunningham always starts off the season slow, but he seems to be hitting his stride now.  His 3-ball is consistently falling as he is shooting 37% from beyond the arc, which is a significant development for his offensive creation abilities and efficiency.

He is going to have to put together another masterclass if the Pistons want any hope to win this game.  During Jalen Duren’s absence, the Pistons have been able to win games through their high-level defense, but their offense has left a lot to be desired.  With Isaiah Joe out and Duncan Robinson going through a bit of a cold stretch, the Pistons shooting fell off a bit and they went four games in a row scoring 110 points or less.

However, everything seemed to get back on track on Monday against the Hornets, so hopefully that continues.

One player the Pistons are hoping gets back on track is John Collins.  He had his best game as a Piston in the last game against the 76ers and has proceeded to score single-digit points in every game since then.  With Jalen Duren out, he has had to play a lot more center than he was probably planning on playing, but he has also had difficulties finding a consistent offensive role.  Another big John Collins game would be a huge help in this matchup

The Joel Embiid matchup concerns me with the Pistons lack of frontcourt size, but if they can defend Tyrese Maxey like they did in the last matchup, they have a shot to takedown the 76ers and claim the top seed in the Eastern Conference.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions confirm Andre Cisco trade; still looking to see if ‘something else makes sense for us’
lions.body:
Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell, left, and general manager Brad Holmes walk off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The NFL trade deadline is set to expire on Tuesday, November 10, at 4 p.m. ET, and while the Detroit Lions have finalized a trade to acquire safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets (and released tight end Jackson Meeks in a corresponding move), coach Dan Campbell said that general manager Brad Holmes “hasn’t stopped” exploring options to upgrade their roster.

While the Lions are getting healthier at safety—with the anticipated return of Kerby Joseph and potentially Thomas Harper—Cisco is a system fit, understands the team’s verbiage from his time with former Lions defensive coordinator turned Jets head coach Aaron Glenn, and helps upgrade the Lions’ secondary as a whole.

“We’ve liked Cisco from afar, having played against him and then even in free agency when he was at Jacksonville coming out,” Campbell said. “So, he’s athletic, he’s versatile. He knows our system. He knows the verbiage. So, we feel like this is a guy that can help us here a little bit. So yeah, we’re excited.”

Beyond the talent Ciasco brings to the field, he also offers the Lions the flexibility to shift some of their existing players’ roles around, meaning a player like rookie Keith Abney, who switched to safety mid-season, could see his role expand back into some work in a more natural nickel role.

“Well, it gives us flexibility,” Campbell continued. “Cisco’s obviously played safety, played nickel. He can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can (Brian) Branch. We get Kerby (Joseph) back eventually here. Kerby gives you flexibility; keep him where you need him or move him back and forth. And then you mentioned Abney. Abney’s got flexibility now: nickel and safety. So, it does. It gives us flexibility, is what it does, and gives us depth too in some regard, wherever that happens at.”

As far as any other potential areas the Lions may want to upgrade, Campbell reiterated that Holmes is exploring options, but it needed to be the right fit at the right price:

“It’s about: is there a piece that could help upgrade us? Is there really, and what is it going to cost you? […] Doesn’t mean that we’re not still looking; see if there’s something else that makes sense for us. But our unit is playing pretty good football right now. [….] And so, it’s got to make sense for us, and it’s got to be something we feel like it can help us, or it gives us significant depth.”

lions.headline: Detroit Lions trade for veteran safety from Jets
lions.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Andre Cisco #8 of the New York Jets talks to teammates in a huddle prior to the game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions are on the board for the 2026 NFL trade deadline.

According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the Lions are trading for New York Jets safety Andre Cisco. In return, the Lions are sending the Jets a 2028 sixth-round pick.

Cisco was drafted in the third round of the 2021 NFL Draft and spent the first four years of his career with the Jacksonville Jaguars. He played in 63 games for the Jaguars, starting 47 games for them over that time. After his rookie deal was up, he signed a one-year, $8.5 million deal with the Jets in 2025 and re-signed with the team on a one-year, $2.5 million deal this offseason.

This season, Cisco has seen his role diminished in New York after starting eight games for them last year. After starting the first three games for the Jets in 2026, Cisco has played a total of just 23 snaps with New York over the past five games.

In Detroit, Cisco should give the Lions some much-needed depth at the safety position. Brian Branch recent returned from his Achilles injury and Kerby Joseph could be on the path to returning now that his practice window has been opened up. However, the Lions have been struggling with their depth at the position. Veteran Chuck Clark has been the primary reserve and has played okay, tallying his second interception of the season on Sunday. But Christian Izien has been benched, Thomas Harper remains on injured reserve, and the Lions have scaled back the work of rookie Keith Abney, who moved to safety midseason. This move could open up the opportunity to move Abney back to nickel cornerback.

As for Cisco, he’s a versatile safety capable of playing both in the box and as a deep, coverage safety. He’ll be appealing to the Lions, because he’s an aggressive run defender. But he also has pretty good ball skills. In college, he tallied 13 interceptions for Syracuse, including seven in his freshman season. At the NFL level, Cisco has eight interceptions, 26 passes defended, four forced fumbles, and 2.5 sacks.

lions.headline: Lions owner Sheila Hamp speaks up in emotional post-game video
lions.body:
We haven’t seen a lot of Detroit Lions owner Sheila Hamp since she took over the team in 2020, but after the team’s emotional win over the Miami Dolphins, she wanted to speak to the team.

It’s been an indescribable week for the Lions. The first half was spent processing their emotions after watching team captain Jack Campbell lie motionless on the Ford Field turf. As the team continued to receive more and more positive updates on Campbell’s condition, the focus shifted back to football and preparing for a gritty Miami Dolphins team. The rallying cry for the week was to prepare and play as Jack Campbell would—with ruthless devotion and an unstoppable work ethic.

After Detroit’s 19-9 victory over the Dolphins, Lions management wanted to commend the players for persevering through the arduous week.

“I’m so proud of you guys. I am unbelievably proud,” coach Dan Campbell said. “For the week that we had, to be able to come in here and finish the way that we finished against a hungry, young team. I’m very proud of you. I really am, man. I love this team. It was built for a reason. The guys that are in this room, you’re in here for a reason—and of course, football players. But it’s what you’re freakin’ made of, men. It’s important.”

Campbell then gave the game ball to Jack Campbell.

Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard also offered some thoughts.

“Nothing about this year has been easy, but leaning on y’all, man? It’s why I wake up every day,” Sheppard said. “It’s why I enjoy that drive to work every day, man. Serving y’all. And offensive guys? Listen, I’d be remiss not to mention y’all, man. How many times y’all [expletive] tapped me during that trial and told me you got me? Well, it was my turn to have y’all. ”

Then Hamp stepped up to deliver a similar message.

“I just want to say how incredibly proud I am of everyone in this room, ” Hamp said. “All you players and the coaches. This has been a hugely emotional week. You all hung together, stuck together, leaned on each other. And look what we did. We won. It was great. I’m so proud of you all.

“I saw Jack a couple days ago, and he was worried about all of you. Well, I know he’s not now. I know he’s as proud of you as I am. So, awesome job. Congratulations. We’re all proud of you and with you.”

lions.headline: Detroit Lions grades: Defensive dominance overshadows offensive line struggles
lions.body:
Detroit Lions linebackers coach Shaun Dion Hamilton talks to linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) after a play Miami Dolphins during the first half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

In the standings, style points do not count. The Detroit Lions’ 19-9 win over the Miami Dolphins counts the same as if the Lions had blown the Dolphins out 38-3.

But in our weekly report cards, we only talk style points. We examine the good and the bad, because life isn’t really just a binary of wins and losses. So let’s hand out some mediocre grades in the Lions’ Week 9 victory.

Quarterback: D+

Jared Goff wasn’t exceptionally bad in this game, but there was probably more bad than good. He was put into some tough positions early with pressure coming from seemingly every angle. It’s hard to fault him for the interception when his arm was hit while throwing, but Goff also didn’t handle the pressure particularly well in this game.

There are two plays in which I think illustrate Goff’s self-made struggles in this game. The first was Detroit’s run-back of the CFL-like play with Amon-Ra St. Brown 15 yards behind the line of scrimmage. The play successfully distracted the Dolphins defense from aptly covering Jahmyr Gibbs’ wheel route of the backfield, but Goff, under mild pressure, didn’t make that throw and checked it down instead. Then, late in the game, the Lions faced a third-and-7 from the Dolphins 25-yard line. With a defender in his face, Goff tried to hit St. Brown on an out route. When at his best, Goff steps into that throw knowing he’s going to get hit and delivers a perfect ball. On Sunday, feeling the effects of the pressure, Goff faded away and delivered a ball several feet beyond St. Brown’s reach.

Again, not a horrible day from Goff, but below average certainly.

Running backs: C-

I thought the running backs did a decent job in pass protection, but there weren’t any standout plays in which it felt like they created any yardage on their own. The Lions managed just 1.55 yards after contract on Sunday, the second-lowest mark of any team in Week 9.

This unit certainly wasn’t helped by the offensive line for much of this game, but I still left the game wanting more from Jahmyr Gibbs and Sione Vaki.

Tight ends: C-

Last week’s “sidecar” formation—with two tight ends in the backfield—was so successful vs. the Vikings. On Sunday, it didn’t seem to have the same effectiveness. There were several times it felt like the tight ends weren’t getting the push they got last week, and I think that impacted both the run and pass game.

That said, Sam LaPorta was an effective receiver that I wish Detroit had targeted more. He caught four of his five targets for 32 yards—though he also had a false start penalty.

Wide receivers: C

Jameson Williams’ drop would’ve been costly had the Lions not followed it up with a successful fake punt. And he made up for it with a 31-yard grab and a 9-yard run. But it was really Amon-Ra St. Brown’s afternoon. He was the team’s best offensive player on Sunday, constantly finding room in the Dolphins’ zone coverage. He finished with eight catches on 10 targets for 86 yards.

Offensive line: D

Christian Mahogany’s violation of team rules proved to be costly, as Miles Frazier struggled in his first NFL start. But he was far from alone in his troubles along the front five. The Lions gave up a 35.5% pressure rate (11th highest of Week 9), but they did at least improve as the game went on:

Q1 pressure rate: 55.6%
Q2: 37.5%
Q3: 14.3%
Q4: 28.6%

This has been an odd trend all year, as pointed out by our own Al Karsten:

Detroit Lions Pass Protection Entering Week 9:

1st Half
• Sack Rate: 9.0% (29th)
• Pressure Rate: 41.7% (24th)

2nd Half
• Sack Rate: 2.5% (3rd)
• Pressure Rate: 29.2% (2nd)

The Dolphins defense entered Week 9 ranked 28th in sack rate (4.1%) and is somehow making life hell…
— Al Karsten (@FootballGuy_Al) November 8, 2026

Frazier and rookie right tackle Blake Miller were the worst offenders on Sunday. Miller allowed three pressures, according to PFF, and Frazier finished with the worst overall grade on the offense (44.1).

But they finished strong, and the Lions were again able to run the clock out on offense on the backs of their offensive line.

Defensive line: A

The Lions absolutely stalled the Dolphins’ rushing attack, holding the Dolphins to just 77 yards and 3.7 yards per carry. Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon had his worst game since September by both rushing yards (55) and yards per carry (3.4). And as a team, the Dolphins had just a 23.8% success rate, ranking 27 out of 28 teams this week, and their 28.6% stuffed rate was third-highest.

While pressure was a little inconsistent with the front four (35.5%, 11th best this week), they came up in big moments. All of Detroit’s three sacks happened in the second half, helping secure their lead.

But the biggest impact of all from this unit cannot be seen easily on the box score. The Lions defensive line helped produce five holding penalties that absolutely killed several Dolphins drives. And if we’re being honest, they probably should have been called for at least a handful more.

Aidan Hutchinson was quietly dominant. Derrick Moore looked extremely promising in his first major action. And Alim McNeill continues to be an absolute force in the middle of the defense.

Linebackers: B+

Without Jack Campbell, it was tough to know how this unit would respond. Consider me very pleasantly surprised. I think Malcolm Rodriguez has been quietly having a very solid year, and he built on that performance in this game. He led the team with eight tackles, was a force in the run game, and had an impressive punchout on a third-down pass, preventing a conversion.

Trevor Nowaske may be the most trustworthy coverage linebacker on the team right now. On 15 coverage snaps, he wasn’t even targeted.

Derrick Barnes continues to be more up and down than the rest of the room. There are still some coverage lapses that are concerning, but this was one of his best games as a run defender, and he tallied a QB hit, as well.

Defensive backs: B

The Lions are still clearly trying to figure some things out in the cornerback room, especially without D.J. Reed in this game. I think Rock Ya-Sin is slowly coming back into form, and he put up a strong performance against the Dolphins. But against this young Dolphins receiving corps, I was hoping for more out of the likes of Roger McCreary and Ennis Rakestraw. McCreary probably got the worst of it, credited by PFF as allowing four catches on seven targets for 49 yards—and he also allowed a deep completion that was luckily negated by a holding penalty.

That said, this is the best game the Lions have gotten from their safety duo. Brian Branch was quiet, but steady working near the line of scrimmage. And Chuck Clark was essentially flawless as the deep defender. His interception was an impressively athletic play, and his return put Detroit immediately into field goal range.

Chuck Clark picked it off! pic.twitter.com/I98vZOuzbq
— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 8, 2026

Special teams: C

A lot going on in special teams this week. The good: Jake Bates was a perfect 5-for-5 on his kicks, Jack Fox dropped his one punt inside the 15-yard line, Fox converted a fake punt with a great throw to Tay Martin, and the coverage teams were fine.

However, Bates kicked one kickoff short of the landing zone and placed another kickoff in the end zone for a 35-yard touchback. Christian Izien committed a holding penalty that erased some good field position on punt return. And worst of all, the Lions allowed a massive 46-yard pass on a fake punt from Miami.

In the end, I think it all evens out for an average grade.

Coaching: A-

I think the coaching staff deserves a ton of credit for navigating an extremely difficult week. The emotions from Jack Campbell’s traumatic injury could not be easy to process and get the team ready to go, but clearly the Lions found a successful balance. They opened Wednesday’s meeting by putting football completely aside and talking through their emotions about Campbell. They downgrade Wednesday’s practice to a walkthrough. Life was more important than football, and they believed they could turn the page with the remaining shortened week. And they did.

There’s not much about the game in terms of play-calling, game management, or anything else that I had any issues with. I don’t put much of the offensive issues on Drew Petzing, as clearly the offensive line losing their one-on-ones had the biggest impact on the struggles.

I supposed we can complain about Dan Campbell’s decision to punish Christian Mahogany and how it hurt this team’s ability to perform. But without knowing Mahogany’s actions that caused the punishment, I cannot fairly judge whether it was the right decision. That said, I’m okay with the coaching staff erring on the side of upholding the strict culture here.

lions.headline: NFC playoff picture: Detroit Lions get no help again
lions.body:
MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions celebrates after an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on November 8, 2026 in (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions are on a four-game winning streak. They’re 6-2 for the third time in last four seasons. They’re 2-0 in divisional play, and are tied in the conference for the best record against NFC opponents (4-1).

Yet, they are still stuck at third in the division and sitting with the six seed in the NFL playoff picture through Week 9 (with “Monday Night Football” still pending).

It’s a frustrating spot to be in, but the good news is that if the Lions can just continue to take care of business, everything is still in front of them. Let’s take a closer look at the NFC playoff picture and what it means for the Lions.

NFC North standings

Minnesota Vikings: 6-1 (2-1 in division)

Chicago Bears: 7-2 (0-2)

Detroit Lions: 6-2 (2-0)

Green Bay Packers: 6-3 (1-2)

The Bears and Packers didn’t just win on Sunday, they looked darn good. The Packers blew out a Patriots team that was starting to look like an AFC Super Bowl contender. They had their first explosive offensive game of the season (45 points, 478 yards), and their defense was opportunistic with three interceptions and four sacks.

Meanwhile, the Bears jumped all over the Buccaneers early on Sunday night. And while a four-interception game from Caleb Williams kept the Bucs in it late, his two-minute drill was all Chicago needed to put the game away.

The good news is that the Minnesota Vikings will have their hands full on Monday night against the Buffalo Bills. If they lose that game, the Vikes will drop to third place in the division, technically tied with Detroit, but the Lions have the head-to-head tiebreaker.

NFC playoff picture

Division leaders:

49ers: 7-1

Vikings: 6-1

Giants: 5-2-1

Panthers: 3-5

Wild Card leaders (top three advance)

5. Bears: 7-2
6. Lions: 6-2
7. Packers: 6-3

8. Seahawks: 5-4
9. Rams: 5-4
10. Cowboys: 4-5
11. Saints: 3-5
12. Buccaneers: 3-6
13. Falcons: 3-6
14. Cardinals: 3-6
15. Commanders: 2-5-1
16. Eagles: 2-7

Miraculously, every NFC team seeded from 1-11 won this week, with the exception of the Carolina Panthers (lost to Broncos) and the Minnesota Vikings (haven’t played yet). So not only did the Lions fail to climb any spots in the playoff race, but they didn’t create any space between them and most of the teams behind them. They still remain 1.5 games ahead of the Seahawks and Rams—and neither of those teams were very convincing in their wins—but it’s still annoying to have such a good record and not feel completely safe in their playoff standing. That said, it’s not all that uncommon. The Cincinnati Bengals are in a pretty similar situation in the AFC, holding an identical 6-2 record and the six seed.

Now, if the Vikings lose on Monday night, the Lions will slide up to the five seed, while the Bears would overtake to two seed and Minnesota would drop to the six seed. Let’s hope the football gods can offer at least one sacrifice this week.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Patriots odds: Opening lines for Week 10 matchup
lions.body:
Nov 10, 2024; Munich, Germany; A large helmet with the 2024 NFL Munich Game logo at Allianz Arena. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con

Seid ihr bereit für etwas Football?

The Detroit Lions (6-2) are headed to Munich, Germany, to take on the New England Patriots (5-4) in an overseas edition of Week 10 NFL Football. It’s been 11 seasons since the Lions last played an international game, but this trip has been in the works for some time.

In 2024, as part of the NFL’s Global Markets Program, the Lions have had marketing rights in the DACH region, which includes Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Since then, the team has made several trips to Germany and has helped support Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown—whose mother, Miriam Brown, was born and raised in Germany—in running youth football programs across the country.

As for the game itself, it looks like it’ll be a good one, and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -2.5 points.

While the Lions are riding a four-game winning streak, the Patriots’ 2026 season has been a more up-and-down affair after reaching the Super Bowl in 2025. They opened the season by losing to the Seahawks, beat the Steelers, then lost to the Jaguars over the first three weeks. They got back to 2-2 with a big win over the Bills, then rallied to 4-2 after wins over the Raiders and Jets. The Bears took them down on Thursday night in Week 7, but the Patriots eeked out a five-point win over the Dolphins to reach 5-3.

On Sunday, the Patriots took on the Packers and looked completely unprepared. Packer QB Jordan Love jumped all over them, throwing for 372 yards and three scores, while Patriots Drake Maye threw for 299 yards and three scores, but also threw three interceptions and was sacked four times. On the ground, the Packers’ worst-ranked rushing offense ran for 129 yards and two touchdowns, while the Pats gained 94 rushing yards, a touchdown, and lost a fumble.

In the end, the Packers left Foxborough with a 45-27 win, and left former Patriots QB and current color commentator Tom Brady wondering who this New England team actually is:

“Half the season they played like this, and the other half of the season they haven’t turned the ball over, they haven’t exposed the defense, have played more physical on defense, but right now it’s just too inconsistent. Which team are they going to get? The team that is loose with the ball, is loose with decision-making, looking like they can be beaten by anybody. Or the team that takes care of the football, that makes the other team play left-handed, and can do what they want to do. Can they be a good team? They haven’t quite done that because good teams leave the smallest margin of error.”

The Lions and Patriots are scheduled to play on Sunday, November 15, at 9:30 a.m. ET at Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany.

lions.headline: Discussion: Are you concerned about the Detroit Lions’ offense?
lions.body:
Nov 8, 2026; Miami Gardens, Florida, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) scrambles for yards during the first half against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Lions are winning, but one thought has lingered in my mind: should these games be this close?

The Lions are up to 6-2 on the season and have now won four games in a row, yet there has been a tonal shift with this team. To start the season, the Lions’ offense was on a tear, scoring 164 points across their first five games (32.8 points scored per game). However, that was offset by a defense that was giving up just as many points (33.8 points allowed per game), leading to a disappointing record of just 3-2 at the bye.

Things have picked of a late for the defense, but the same cannot be said about the offense. Across their past three games, the Lions have scored just 20 points versus the Green Bay Packers, 19 points versus the Minnesota Vikings, and 19 points against the Miami Dolphins. Early in the season, this would have meant three-straight losses, but some stout defensive showings (allowing just 17, 15, and 9 points across those games) have kept Detroit on a win streak.

Head coach Dan Campbell has often preached the importance of complementary football. The defense has stepped up in recent weeks, but the offense is suddenly and surprisingly lagging behind. After a torrid start to the season, what is up with the offense?

Today’s Question of the Day is:

Are you concerned about the Detroit Lions’ offense?

My answer: No.

The Lions offense has had some lackluster moments against the Packers, Vikings, and Dolphins, without question. However, I think that the ceiling of this offense shines through enough to ease my worries—the offense is in a lull, not a fall. There are two drives in particular that I want to highlight that show how good this offense can be.

Firstly, I want to address the Lions’ second drive of the fourth quarter versus the Vikings. Minnesota had just scored a touchdown to put themselves up 15-12. With just under eight minutes left in the game, the Lions not only had to mount a scoring drive, but also eat up enough time to make things uncomfortable for the Vikings when they got the ball back. The Lions wound up going on a seven-play, 69-yard touchdown drive to eat up four minutes of clock.

What truly stood out about that drive was the presence that Detroit brought. Throughout most of the game, Detroit had struggled to run the ball. Jahmyr Gibbs had scored on a 30-yard scamper earlier in the third quarter, but aside from that, we had not seen the dominant run game that Detroit was known for. That changed on this drive. Detroit started churned out yards with ease—carries of 17 yards, 12 yards, 10 yards, and two 9-yarders made up the bulk of the drive. Detroit enacted their will against the Vikings defense and ran the ball down their throat. That was vintage Lions football under Dan Campbell.

Secondly, the lone touchdown drive versus the Dolphins this week: it was a thing of beauty. Most of us would agree that the Lions had left plenty of points off the board on Sunday. They settled for a lot of field goals, particularly due to some ill-timed negative plays on third downs—Detroit would have had to take a significant risk forego a kick. Miami had not been threatening, but time was running out for Detroit to net themselves a more comfortable lead.

Whereas the drive versus the Vikings was them dominating in the trenches, this drive versus the Dolphins showed how explosive the offense can be. Right off the bat, Jared Goff hits Jameson Williams deep for 31 yards. The very next play, he hits Amon-Ra St. Brown for 17 yards. The following plays gained 5 and 4 yards. Suddenly in the blink of an eye, Detroit has marched down the field to score. Thankfully on this drive, they finished it, as Gibbs sprinted around linebacker Jordyn Brooks for the touchdown.

That ended as a six-play, 65-yard drive in just two minutes and 40 seconds. It looked easy. That is the genuinely scary thing about this offense: when they are on point, nobody can stop them. The Lions have a plethora of weapons, a reliable and tough-as-nails quarterback, and a creative play caller—this is a combination few teams can stop.

When it works.

Whenever I look at this offense, I do not see a team devoid of talent (like the Dolphins). I do not see a team suffering from horrendous decision-making (like the Los Angeles Chargers). More often than not, the only team capable of stopping the offense is the offense itself. Look back to that game against the Cardinals. Even the best offenses in the league rarely look as dominant as Detroit did in that game. Scoring 45 points is certainly an outlier, but the offense genuinely has the mettle to make that a weekly threat.

I would love to see the Lions score earlier in games to cement more comfortable leads, but I think the offense nonetheless passes the eye test. I think Petzing is an adaptive play caller and knows how to get the best out of his players. As an example, a week after running the creative 15-yard-deep screen, they lined up St. Brown in that same look but instead threw the ball elsewhere—the team knows how to zig one week then zag the next. Part of what makes Petzing a good coordinator is that he takes what does not work during a game and adapts in the moment. I trust him to get the offense out of a hole.

Is the Lions’ offense perfect? Certainly not. However, I think their recent low-scoring affairs do not tell the whole story. I still feel confident in the team’s talent and creativity, and they have shown enough flashes on a weekly basis to instill plenty of faith. Do you agree with me? Let us know in the comments below.

michigan.headline: ‘It never clicked’: Kyle Whittingham explains what went wrong under Jason Beck
michigan.body:
Michigan offensive coordinator Jason Beck looks over his play call sheet during the second half at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Michigan State beat Michigan 15-6. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Following the firing of offensive coordinator Jason Beck, Michigan Wolverines head coach Kyle Whittingham explained what went wrong with the offense this season and why it was time to make a change at a press conference on Monday.

“It never clicked,” Whittingham told the media. “We never seemed to get into a rhythm. He’s the offensive coordinator, so things fall on his plate as far as the responsibility for the lack of production, so that’s why we had to make the change.”

Michigan’s offense was undoubtedly among the nation’s worst units under Beck, currently ranking 132nd in yards per game (302.6), 125th in points per game (19.6), 124th in first downs per game (16.9) and 123rd in yards per play (4.8).

It doesn’t get much worse than that, as the Wolverines struggled to find any glimmer of success for most of the season. Beck came into his first season at Michigan with high expectations, but instead, he was fired following just nine games.

Beck was certainly on the hot seat heading into last week’s rivalry game against the Michigan State Spartans, and by the time the game ended, it only felt like a matter of time until the first-year offensive coordinator was going to be fired.

“We didn’t do anything well on Saturday,” Whittingham said. “We didn’t run the ball well enough, we didn’t throw it well enough, we didn’t convert third downs, we didn’t protect the quarterback, and the biggest thing was four turnovers.”

Whittingham is right. Michigan’s offense didn’t do one thing right in a truly embarrassing 15-6 loss to Michigan State, who was winless and in last place in the Big Ten. So it became abundantly clear that it was time to move on from Beck.

The final nail in Beck’s coffin was a disaster-class against Michigan State, unlike any we’ve ever seen, as Michigan put up a nauseating 192 total yards and 3.7 yards per play, while committing four turnovers and finishing 2-for-10 on third downs.

According to the Associated Press’ Josh Dubow, Michigan was held scoreless in the first half of three separate home games this season, which had only happened a total of three times in the previous 24 years. Yeah, I think Beck had to go.

“Watching the film was the deciding factor,” Whittingham said. “I had the intention of waiting until after the season, but when I turned on the film, it was apparent I needed to make a change now. There was too much regression on offense.”

Whether it be a disparity in play calling and personnel, lack of understanding of Big Ten defenses, or a flawed scheme, Beck’s offense never clicked at Michigan, and Whittingham eventually had no choice but to fire the offensive coordinator.

michigan.headline: Roster retention talks are ‘already in progress’ for Michigan Football
michigan.body:
Sep 12, 2026; Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; Michigan Wolverines head coach Kyle Whittingham reacts to a call during the first quarter against the Oklahoma Sooners at Michigan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Michigan’s 2026 football season was all but lost over the weekend, with the Wolverines suffering a 15-6 defeat to in-state rival Michigan State. The Spartans came to town winless in Big Ten play and dealing with their own set of struggles, but still found a way to hand Michigan its most crippling loss of the year.

It’s been slowly building over the course of the season, but with each passing week, it’s become more apparent that Kyle Whittingham and much of his coaching staff didn’t know what they were signing up for when they were hired. The offense had been particularly troublesome (choose your own adjective), and it has resulted in offensive coordinator Jason Beck being fired on Sunday despite being one of the highest-paid assistants in the country.

Beck’s firing came too late in the year to make any sort of meaningful change, but that doesn’t mean Whittingham and those around the program were content to sit idly by and watch things continue to crumble.

When speaking with reporters at his press conference on Monday morning, Whittingham added that the efforts to right the ship have also included talks about roster retention and keeping the 2027 recruiting class together amid what’s been a highly disappointing season.

“Those conversations are already in progress,” Whittingham said of trying to get players on the roster back with the program next year. “We’ve had going back weeks and weeks personnel meetings and talking about players that we definitely need to try to keep.”

Whittingham didn’t characterize this as an admission of punting on the remaining three games, but rather that retention efforts are ramping up as the season’s winding down so as not to be a “distraction” earlier in the year. Sitting at 5-4 with games against Oregon, UCLA and Ohio State looming, the writing is on the wall that Michigan could miss a bowl game, signaling the need to get a jump on preparing for next year.

With Beck now gone, there would also be concerns about keeping the 2027 class together, particularly on offense. Most notably, four-star quarterback commit Kamden Lopati was at Utah on Saturday to watch the Utes defeat BYU in the Holy War.

Holy War, what a game! @Utah_Football is building something special and I was grateful to witness it. Thank you for the hospitality.@J2theGross @RSNBUtes @MasonYellicoUT @coachdoraz @GregBiggins @SamLeSueur @Andy_Pham1 @247recruiting @BlairAngulo @BrandonHuffman @On3Recruiting pic.twitter.com/9DEilcutQN
— Samiu Taukiuvea (@SamiuTaukiuvea) November 8, 2026

Whittingham said he called every commit in the 2027 class on Sunday night amid the program’s turmoil this fall.

While it’s encouraging Whittingham still has an eye on the future, especially with this season’s team going nowhere fast, it’s fair to wonder if this effort is even worthwhile since it’s not clear whether Whittingham will be back next season. After losing to hapless Michigan State over the weekend, calls from the fan base to fire him reached a fever pitch, and Michigan should certainly consider moving on.

Michigan currently doesn’t have an athletic director set up to take over for Warde Manuel at the end of the year, and new president C. Cybele Raver doesn’t officially start until Dec. 1, a few days after the 2026 season’s conclusion and right in the middle of the prime time on the college football calendar for coaching changes. That shouldn’t (and probably wouldn’t) prevent the university’s biggest boosters or Board of Regents from taking matters into their own hands, but it is worth keeping in mind at least.

Regardless of where things end up a few weeks from now, Michigan has to start planning for what the program looks like beyond this season, and getting the ducks in a row with the roster is a good place to start.

Late Saturday night I had a daydream in which C Cybele Raver, the new president of the university, tore into the locker room after the game. Mildly disheveled after an altercation with a security guard who did not know she was his boss's boss's boss, an incensed Raver would cause a clatter as she entered, alarming the funereal locker room. There, a breath. After, Raver points directly at Kyle Whittingham, saying "you're fired"—now, in one smooth motion her other hand is coming out from behind her back(!) to point elsewhere—and this elsewhere happens to be Jason Beck—and then she says "you're fired, too!" Woo! Yowza! Hot stuff! But ALSO! Not done, she points at Jay Hill and says "interim" and then LEAVES THE FUCKING ROOM TO GO CALL BOB CHESNEY.
Phew. Wow. I mean.
Powerful stuff. I'm gonna do one of those little things with lots of minuses to emphasize this. The above is meaningful. Yeah.
------------------------------------------------
Yesterday part of this did transpire. Michigan fired Jason Beck. Why is simultaneously obvious and obscure. The obvious part is obvious. The obscure part is that after maybe the worst football game played in Michigan Stadium, Whittingham stated flat-out that he was not going to replace Beck:
Michigan HC Kyle Whittingham on if something has to change with Jason Beck:

That is around the same time the lame duck athletic director will give way to someone else. Right now there does not appear to be anyone actually in charge of making decisions about Kyle Whittingham. Maybe Beck approached Whittingham like a guy in a movie who's been hit with a lethal dose of radiation and asked to be put out of his misery. Whatever it is, Beck is gone. This seems to have satiated no Michigan fans, including myself. There is no amount of doing what I want that will satiate me at this point. Whittingham's proclamations that Jason Beck was doing bad football after games was charmingly honest the first time; since it has been an admission that he's just along for the ride.
The silver lining, such as it is, is that things are so bad that it feels impossible for Michigan to not make the unprecedented decision to dump their head football coach after just one season. The fanbase is ready to riot. When Michigan called a Bryson Kuzdzal run on third and eight the stadium exploded with the most noise they'd made all night.
This is when I turned to my son and asked him if he wanted to go.
-----------------------------------------
He's ten. This was his third game, and the first real one—the others were UTEP and the like. By the end of the third quarter he had been saying he was really cold, and after that I couldn't justify immiserating my son further for a team that wasn't even trying to win.
As we were walking out I heard Doug Karsch describe the illegal substitution penalty on Michigan State and the subsequent completion to Buchanan at the 50. I heard a roar of some variety a minute later and assumed that I'd done it again. I left the Western game when the clock said zero the first time. I envisioned that Michigan had contrived to score a touchdown and felt bad about leaving a still-competitive game.
I got home to see Michigan State kicking a field goal to go up 9-0. A quick catch up showed me… I don't even know what. I was so jaded looking at it. A Kuzdzal fumble or something. I stared blankly and regretting forcing my son to do this thing, though he seemed happy enough to have done it.
It's funny how my mind snapped to something other than the grim reality of the program right now. I was dispirited to find out the truth, but also relieved. This is never going to work because Utah was right to move on from Whittingham when they did. The clearer that is to the mysterious Powers That Be, the quicker we can move on from the hideous denouement of Warde Manuel's tenure at Michigan.
There's no flicker of hope here. Beck's firing isn't a sea change; Michigan will be equally miserable with or without him for the rest of the season. The real question is whether there's anyone in charge enough to do what needs to be done so Michigan can have a normal coaching search for the first time since Dave Brandon hired Brady Hoke.
I doubt it, and I don't know how I'm supposed to sell my kid on the idea that football is worth paying attention to. I'm not even sure I'm sold on that idea right now.
[THERE IS NO CONTENT AFTER THE JUMP]

michigan.headline: What Kyle Whittingham is looking for in Michigan Football’s next offensive coordinator
michigan.body:
Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham watches a play against Indiana during the first half at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Michigan Wolverines fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck on Sunday, as the offense continued to play poorly over the weekend and only put up six points and 178 total yards of offense in the 15-6 loss to MSU.

This upcoming offseason, head coach Kyle Whittingham will be tasked with hiring a new offensive coordinator. He spoke to the media on Monday about what he’s looking for in his next offensive coordinator.

“A proven play caller with a track record of success,” Whittingham said. “It would be great if they had Michigan or Midwest ties, and know the landscape and the conference. Also an excellent leader. That’s always at the top of the list.”

Michigan could be an attractive job for offensive coordinators across the country, and Whittingham is going to target someone that is a proven play caller and is a quality leader. It doesn’t sound like the next offensive coordinator necessarily has to have a connection to Michigan or the Big Ten, but it sounds like it would be a bonus if they were. Still, the most important quality is an experienced play caller with prior success.

Beck had multiple years of experience calling plays, but he is still relatively young and wasn’t exactly proven quite yet. Whittingham will likely go after someone that comes with more experience and has called plays for more than a few years.

“It was a tough tough call but it’s part of the process,” Whittingham said. “My job is to make decisions I believe are in the best interest of the program, no matter how difficult it is. I owe it to the program to do what’s best for the program.”

It’s certainly very difficult to make any predictions at this point in time, but when Whittingham detailed what he’s looking for in the search for a new offensive coordinator, two names popped into my head: current Northwestern offensive coordinator Chip Kelly and Notre Dame offensive coordinator Mike Denbrock.

Kelly and Denbrock both fit Whittingham’s description to a tee. It would likely be hard to lure them away from their current respective positions or other opportunities they could be offered this offseason, but it definitely doesn’t hurt to try.

Denbrock is a Michigan native that has coached for nearly four decades, including being an offensive coordinator at Cincinnati, LSU, and now, Notre Dame. It’s unclear if he would leave Notre Dame for another coordinator job, but he does fit Whittingham’s vision.

Meanwhile, Kelly is one of the nation’s premier offensive coordinators, with successful stints at Ohio State and Oregon before turning around Northwestern’s offense this year. Could Whittingham convince him to make a move to Ann Arbor?

It’s not a certainty that Whittingham, himself, will even return next year, but if he does, the offensive coordinator hire will make or break his tenure at Michigan. Beck was a failure in Ann Arbor, so Whittingham’s next hire has to be a home run.
