Researching into how bad have things gotten for Michigan, motivated by the discussion during the podcast about "we have a 5* QB and a 5* RB, not just for this year but historically rated top players". I used some AI to assemble a listing of "Efficient" teams, essentially taking points per game and dividing by composite recruiting rankings for the roster (AI used PPG/247 Sports Talent score * 100). The Top 10 teams for this year are:

North Texas 11.46
Army 10.50
Navy 10.4
JMU 9.9
FAU 9.46
Other teams scoring well where they're not skewed toward mid majors with low recruiting rankings include Boise St (6.72) Miami (5.36), Indiana (4.75), and Georgia (4.1).
Obviously, Michigan is nowhere close, but how bad is it?
Michigan has a score of 2.20. I asked for the bottom teams in this metric, and the AI inverted the metric to score "inefficient teams" (Talent score / PPG). Your ranking:

Michigan 41.98
Oklahoma 39.77
Wisconsin 39.87
Florida St 34.93
Auburn 33.53
Texas A&M 32.42
So yeah, this passes the sniff test. Now how bad are we in historical context? I asked for top inefficient teams in college football since 2000... the list is.. not great Bob. Titles in quotes were provided by AI:
"The all time standard": 2022 Texas A&M... highest rated recruiting class in history, collapsed to a 5-7 record, only scoring 22.8 ppg. Their inefficiency rating = 41.35
"The total collapse": 2018 Florida State... Willie Taggert's first year after Jimbo left for TAMU. Finished 5-7. Averaged 21.9 ppg. Inefficiency rating = 38.1
"The modern comparison": 2023 IOWA HAWKEYES. From AI "Unlike Texas A&M or FSU, Iowa does not recruit top-5 classes. However, because their scoring output was so jaw-droppingly historic, they broke the math... Even though their roster wasn't loaded with five-stars, the point output was so historically low that they required more "talent units" per point scored than almost anyone". Averaged 15.4 ppg on way to a.... 10-4 record. Inefficiency rating: 44.80
So we are trending toward some historically laughable program collapse years (Jimbo's TAMU probably the most equivlaent) that led to HC firings. We will probably (maybe?) not be on 2023 Iowa Hawkeye levels, but the potential is there.

michigan.headline: This Week on State Street Knows It’s Too Late to Fix This
michigan.body:
This Week on State Street Knows It’s Too Late to Fix This

ByAZuniga
November 9th, 2026 at 1:03 PM

In the minutes after the Michigan State debacle, during which the Wolverines were shut out for more than 58 minutes by a below-average defense, Kyle Whittingham said potential changes to the coaching staff wouldn’t come until the offseason. Less than 24 hours later, Michigan reversed course, firing Jason Beck and promising a national search for the program’s next offensive coordinator.
The question of who fired Beck seems significant, insofar as it tells us whether this regime will have any longevity or hope of success in Ann Arbor. If this was Whittingham’s decision, and his alone, it suggests some level of adaptability, of understanding when things aren’t working and taking corrective action. On the other hand, if intervention from Warde Manuel and/or other stakeholders forced Whittingham into unwanted action, that points to a fracture among leadership that may be too deep to repair.
Whittingham would like you to believe it was his call.
“Zero outside influence,” he said, explaining the move came based on “my own analysis, my own feel, my own gut instinct.”
Jim Harding will take over as interim offensive coordinator, which will make his weeks particularly busy given he’s still in charge of an injury-riddled and struggling offensive line. But with three weeks left in a letdown season, even Whittingham acknowledged it’s too late to overhaul an offense that ranks among the worst in the nation in most statistical categories.
“You can't do major changes at this juncture,” he said. “… You can only do so much at this point in the season, and there will be a few different wrinkles, for sure, but to say there's going to be a complete overhaul, that's not really feasible.”
Even as Michigan prepares for a road game at a top-20 opponent, conversation has already turned to next year. Whittingham spoke of the staff intensifying roster-retention efforts, and that they’ve identified “exactly what we need” from their next recruiting/Transfer Portal class.
Bigger picture, Michigan is in the midst of an athletic director and university president transition. It spent some $12 million on the recent investigation into its athletic department. The Beck buyout could top $10 million. Whittingham’s buyout after one season would be $24.75 million. Rumblings of player discontent indicate Michigan will undergo a significant roster overhaul this season, and that won’t come cheap. Donor fatigue is real.
On the other hand, watching a previously 2-6 Michigan State parade the Paul Bunyan Trophy around the Big House after outclassing the Wolverines might make pulling out the wallet more palatable.
Here’s what you need to know from Kyle Whittingham’s press conference on Monday morning:
Whittingham claims the decision to fire Jason Beck involved “zero outside influence” and came after reviewing the Michigan State film.
Michigan is once again reconsidering its quarterback situation, with the starter against Oregon still TBD.
Blake Frazier is doubtful for the Oregon game after leaving injured against the Spartans.
Conversations with players Michigan wants to retain are “already in progress.”
Hit the jump for PUPPIES, a full transcript, plus some snark:

Kyle Whittingham on why Michigan fired Jason Beck after he said decisions would wait until the offseason:
Well, watching the film really was the deciding factor. I had the intention of waiting until after the season, as I mentioned, but when I turned the film on and really dove into it, it just became apparent to me that we needed to make the change now. There was just too much regression in the offense in that particular game, and that's what led to the decision.
Kyle Whittingham on if there was outside influence in the decision to fire Jason Beck:
Zero. Zero outside influence. You know, just my own analysis, my own feel, my own gut instinct.
AZ: Do I believe this? I do not.
Kyle Whittingham on if Tommy Carr or Bryce Underwood will start against Oregon:
To be determined, but there was consideration about whether to insert Bryce and try to create something [against Michigan State]. And after discussion, it was determined to stay the course with what we had in that particular game, but going forward, we'll take a look at everything again and see what gives us the best chance to win, as it always comes down to that.
AZ: During his postgame press conference after the MSU loss, Whittingham suggested there might be more to the story regarding the decision not to insert Bryce Underwood against the Spartans. But he stopped himself, chuckled and said, "I won't get into that."
Kyle Whittingham on the OL struggles given all 5 starters have played multiple years:
We've got to become more efficient up front. We lost Blake Frazier. He'll be doubtful this week, but there were some encouraging things. Babalola had his first time during the season and played pretty decent. Marky Walbridge came in and played some good reps again, like he had previously.
But we've just got to be better. It's not just the offensive line. That was a game where we didn't play nearly as well as we had hoped to up front, really in any capacity. We didn't run the ball well enough. We didn't protect the quarterback. We had five sacks is what we gave up, so it was a disappointing outing by coaches and a lot of position groups alike. It was not just one thing.
AZ: Fun fact: The City of Ann Arbor Fire Department received a report Saturday about an "offensive line figurative dumpster fire at Michigan Stadium."
Kyle Whittingham on if interim OC Jim Harding will have support given his expanded role:
We already do have that in place. Mike Lynch is Jim's assistant.
AZ: His bio: "Mike Lynch is in his first year assisting with the offensive line at Michigan. He has spent 26 seasons as a position coach and coordinator at the FBS level, working with every offensive position group during his coaching career." He was at Nevada in 2024-25 and previously worked at Syracuse and Bowling Green, among other stops.
Kyle Whittingham on what went into naming Jim Harding the interim OC:
It seemed to me to be the best fit for what we need right now for these last three weeks. He doesn't have extensive play-calling experience, but really nobody on the offensive staff has been in that role, or has been in that role.
Jim is a very good football coach. He's very tuned in to the big picture. He's been with me for a lot of years now, and to me he was the right fit and the right guy to get through these three weeks of the season.
AZ: Maybe Michigan should go full Akron and let fans call the plays in exchange for NIL contributions.
Kyle Whittingham on Oregon’s offense since changing OC:
The quarterback is playing much better. That's the biggest difference. The quarterback has become much more efficient in the last few games, and that was really the issue prior.
I'll tell you what: They're a talented football team. They've got talent across the board, throughout the whole roster. But that's been the biggest difference is the efficiency of the quarterback play in the last couple of weeks.
Kyle Whittingham on if fans should expect major offensive changes this season:
You can't do major changes at this juncture. It will be collaborative, and it had been collaborative. It's never just a one-man show.
You can only do so much at this point in the season, and there will be a few different wrinkles, for sure, but to say there's going to be a complete overhaul, that's not really feasible.
Kyle Whittingham on if he’ll become more involved in the offensive play calling:
No. I’ll leave it up to the offensive coaches. I'll obviously be aware of what's going on, and what we're doing schematically, and personnel, and all that type of thing, but that's not my role to be a play caller, so no, I don't anticipate that being any different.
Kyle Whittingham on what about the Michigan State film led to the Jason Beck decision:
We didn't do much of anything very well on Saturday night. You can go down the entire list: Didn't run the ball well enough; didn't throw it well enough; didn't make enough third-down conversions; didn't protect the quarterback.
But the biggest thing is four turnovers. We were minus-four in the turnover margin. Really, nothing else matters beyond that. If you're minus-four, you have a 95% chance of losing, regardless of what else happens. That was the most glaring and disappointing factor, was the way we didn't take care of the football.
AZ: Michigan ranks 132nd of 138 FBS teams in turnover margin.
Kyle Whittingham on his impressions of Big Ten defenses:
First of all, let's start with our defense. I think they're playing exceptionally well. It wasn't our best game Saturday night, but any time you don't give up a touchdown, that's a pretty good thing to have happen. We were a little soft on a couple of drives. They had a couple of long drives on us, but the red zone defense was outstanding: 0-for-4 in the red zone against Michigan State. The defense is what kept us in the game and has what has kept us in games all season long. Those guys are playing hard. They're playing smart. You can see guys flying around.
We weren't perfect. Missed some tackles. Had a chance at a couple of takeaways, but didn't get it done. Very proud of what they've done so far this year. I think we're 4th or 5th in the country in total defense, which is admirable.
Defenses in the Big Ten overall: Good, physical. A lot of similarities — even front, quarters coverage in the back end. There's not a ton of variation, at least what we've seen so far. Oregon will be very similar as well. 'Physicality' is probably the operative word for defenses in the Big Ten.
Kyle Whittingham on what can change with the offense in what remains of the season:
Play more efficiently up front. That's where it starts. Play more efficiently at the quarterback position. As good as Tommy played two weeks ago, there was a big drop-off in this game with the efficiency. He'll be the first one to tell you that. Missed quite a few throws that were very makeable throws and completions that should have been had. Again, it's a combination of things, but you might see some things a little bit different in the throw game.
But again, it can't be a wholesale change. Just subtle changes here and there, formational changes, and just different ways to attack in general.
AZ: It turns out that extrapolating one game's worth of data against Rutgers across an entire season is not appropriate. As Austin Meek of The Athletic wrote: It "suggests a fundamental misunderstanding of 'Rutgers,' both as a concept and as a football program."
Kyle Whittingham on what he’d like to see from Michigan's offense against Oregon:
More production on offense. That's the obvious issue and has been in our losses this year. It's really been a lack of ability to put points on the board and control the football. People have done a good job winning the time of possession against us for a lot of games this year. But yeah, we've got to become more efficient.
And special teams: We need to make more of an impact there. We haven't had much of an impact either way. It hasn't been bad, but we haven't had those big special teams plays where we create a takeaway or big returns. And so that would help our cause as well, if we can get more production in the special teams aspect.
Kyle Whittingham on why Jason Beck didn’t work at Michigan after his success elsewhere:
It's a good question. It just never seemed to click here. We never seemed to get in a rhythm. At times, there were some stretches where we played pretty good.
And again, I want to make the point that it's not all Jason. Anytime you have issues like we have, it's more than just one guy. But he's the offensive coordinator. Things fall on his plate as far as the responsibility for the production or lack thereof of the offense. And so that's why we made the change. But it's got to be a collaborative effort by everybody to get this thing going in the direction we need it to go.
Kyle Whittingham on the conversation with Jason Beck and the reaction from the players:
I don't want to get into what the conversation was like. That's really nobody's business but mine and Jason's.
Players' reaction: We'll have a team meeting today, so we haven't had them all together since the move. And so I can't really give you a great answer to that one. I know in meetings this morning, individual meetings, the players were disappointed, obviously, in the game. But they're a very prideful group and they're very competitive. And so I wouldn't say anybody's hanging their head or sulking. But probably disappointed and embarrassed is probably better terms to use.
Kyle Whittingham on how he’d evaluate the current class Michigan has on offense:
I'm not going to get into that specifically. But I can just say we're very excited to be able to put a class together and have a recruiting cycle. We didn't get here until January and the recruiting cycle was pretty much over with. We did spend time trying to retrieve guys out of the Portal. That was our biggest project: When we got here, half the team seemingly was in the Portal. And we were trying to get them back out of it, which we succeeded in partially. We were able to get quite a few of the players back.
It's going to be our job and our responsibility now to continue to build the roster through recruiting the guys that we want in this program. And we've got a really good start on that. We've got a lot of positive things going on in the ’27 class. It's still two or three weeks away from Signing Day. But we feel like we know exactly what we need and exactly what needs to take place in recruiting.
Kyle Whittingham on how he addresses the coaching changes with recruits:
We got on the phone with every recruit last night. And they seemed to be very receptive and positive. Nobody was panicking. Nobody was saying, ‘Well, coach, I don't know about my commitment now,’ and so forth.
First of all, it's Michigan. And you come to Michigan for a lot of reasons. Academics, the tradition, the history. Coaching changes are a part of college football. And they go on constantly. There's been several coordinator changes, head coach changes so far this year. And there's going to be a lot more, I can tell you that. And so that's just part of the deal.
If you're looking to go to a place that never has change or turnover, that's fantasy land. That doesn't exist.
Kyle Whittingham on shrugging off the ‘embattled coach’ label:
That's the furthest thing from my mind. I could care less about any of that. My focus is doing the best job I can to try to get this program back to where it needs to be. And that's it. And I have no concern other than that. Zero. And that's a fact. Some coaches say that and they really do have concern. I have no concern. Trust me.
AZ: and another thing: im not mad. please dont put in the newspaper that i got mad
Kyle Whittingham on if it was difficult to move on from Jason Beck:
Very tough. It's a tough call, but that's part of the process. Part of the job is making those tough decisions. My job is to make decisions that I believe are in the best interest of the program, no matter how difficult they may be.
You've got to put personal feelings aside because I really like Jason Beck. He's a great person. He's a loyal guy that I just think is just a terrific guy. It was not easy, but I've had to do it before. That's the nature of the business. You've got to do what's best. I owe it to the program to do what's best for the program. Period.
Kyle Whittingham on what he’s looking for from Michigan’s next offensive coordinator:
A proven play-caller. A proven track record of success. It would be great if there was Michigan ties or at least Midwest ties. Someone that knows the landscape and the conference. An excellent leader of young men. That's always going to be right at the top of the list as being a role model and leader for the guys in the program.
AZ: Michigan offensive coordinator Chip Kelly? He's got to continue his tour of the Big Ten somewhere...
Kyle Whittingham on if Michigan successfully built its offensive scheme around the players on the roster:
I'm not going to make excuses. We were glad to get the players back that we did get back. I wish we could have gotten a few more back.
In college football, 95% of the snaps in college football are spread from the shotgun. There's far more similarities than differences in offenses throughout the country. I'm not going to use that as an excuse that we didn't have the right players for the personnel. As a coach, you've got to make it work. You've got to make it fit. You can't just say, ‘Here's what we're doing on offense, period. We're not going to be flexible with it. We're going to be very rigid.’ You've got to be able to adapt to your personnel. We just didn't do a good job of that this year. Plain and simple.
Kyle Whittingham on if there’s a disconnect between he and the coaching staff not understanding the bigger picture of Michigan:
The big picture is winning. That's the picture. That's where it starts. That's where it ends. I'm not sure what you're alluding to or what you're saying here.
Kyle Whittingham on the decision to fire Jason Beck coming later than fans wanted:
If you listen to the fans, you're going to be sitting with them, is the old adage. I've got to do what's best for the program without trying to please anybody. I'm trying to position the program in the best possible way to be successful. I can't take a poll of the fans or whatever else is out there.
We respect our fans, and they've been supportive all year. Grateful they come out and cheer our players on. That's all great. But as far as in-house decisions and decisions I've got to make, I don't really think that's part of the equation.
Kyle Whittingham on if Michigan is already actively trying to retain players:
Those conversations are already in progress. Yeah, absolutely. The Portal is what, January 2, I think is when it opens. And so yeah, we are already. And we've had going back weeks and weeks, personnel meetings and talking about the players that we definitely need to try to keep on board. That is ongoing as a staff, pretty much year-round.
But with players, yeah, it's just been recently that we've been starting to have those conversations with them. You don't want to be a distraction too early in the season. You've got to wait until the season is winding down. But you can't wait too long because then you're going to miss the boat. Because if you're not talking to your players about it, someone else is.

msu.headline: Sun Finally Shines as MSU Downs Michigan in The Weather Report
msu.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 07: Nick Sharpe #52 of the Michigan State Spartans and the Michigan State Spartans mascot celebrate with the Paul Bunyan Trophy after a 15-6 win over the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Holy expletive! Doth my eyes deceive me? Is this truly an MSU victory? Over the weasels? In their play pen? The answer is yes, yes to all of it. It has been a rough season without a doubt, but to beat Michigan, that is a game all of us would be happy to win. So, we finally have ourselves some real joy for this week’s weather report.

Sun #1

The first sun has to go to Joe Rossi. I mean the man barely has people available to take the field. The defense looked prepared, had a game plan, and executed. Five sacks, four turnovers and a near shutout all against your rival on the road without half of your normal starters is exactly why Rossi gets the sun. Plus the batted down passes, and tackle for losses just added to the reasoning. I loved the intensity and physicality of the defense. The defense has been gritty all year. Not always successful, but they’ve been gritty. They have had a grit that is what Spartan football is supposed to be. This was a special win and this defense deserves a lot of that credit. Now the question is, can a win like this give this team a push for the rest of the season?

Sun #2

My second sun is headed to the kicking game. First and foremost, Liam Boyd was lights out. Every kick mattered and he was as solid as someone could be. The 49 yarder, that could have been good for longer, was a nail in the coffin kick. Boyd wasn’t the only boot that made a difference. Rhys Dakin had some great punts. Only had to punt four times but three of them were inside the 20. That just allowed the defense more opportunity to tee up on the weasels. Let’s also not forget to give a shout out to Jacob Baggett for his beautiful doink off the upright. It was little things like that that gave me hope that we had a chance. Second time this season I’m handing out a sun to Liam Boyd.

Sun #3

I have a shared third sun. My first part is going to the stat sheet and MSU dominating in everything. Time of possession, passing, rushing, turnovers, and as usual against Michigan, penalties. It was a strange feeling to feel there was this chance all game long. Our memory of Northwestern and Illinois made it difficult to keep the hope but ultimately, MSU was in charge this whole game. Part two of this shared sun is going to the booing Michigan fans. There is nothing I love more that hearing weasel fans boo their own team, in their own house. Boo away Ann Arbor, boo your way through all your excuses.

Cloud #1

First cloud goes to the inability to punch it in the end zone. Michigan has a solid defense and one that showed that as it shut MSU out of the end zone for the whole game. MSU was close numerous times but never could cross the line. The Spartans have got to get the ball in the end zone when you get that close. Some of the problem was play calling and some was just being outplayed. Thankfully, MSU still managed to put points up with the field goals.

Cloud #2

Cloud 2 is headed to the 7 penalties because I can finally be a bit picky with the clouds. You have to expect the whistles when playing in the play pen and the 7 penalties were not good. Honestly though, it is hard to make this a cloud because MSU was playing physical and typically would have been called for even more. I’m glad they were getting hands on receivers and fortunate the interference calls or even phantom late hit calls weren’t called to benefit the weasels. So, this is like a half cloud, which leads me to my next conundrum.

Cloud #3…nah Sun #4

I’m sorry my friends but I am too elated to talk negative and my hatred for the opponent has been at unhealthy levels since childhood. So, let’s talk about some more sun. I want to mention some individuals who helped this win. Shout out to Alessio for getting on the field after being questionable all week. Shout out to Chrishon McCray for some big time catches to keep things moving and momentum staying with Sparta. Shout out to Brandon Tullis who had 25 carries for 86 yards. There were not many of those 86 yards that came easy, but he continued to push and at times get just enough. Lastly, a shout out to Coach Fitz. The final score has not always been in our favor but the grit, the handling of adversity, the effort being made to get back to what Spartan football is has been noticed. I know there are plenty that don’t want him here and hated the hire. I think after the way this team has fought each week through all of its adversities is a testament to your coach and I think Fitz deserves some credit for that and a bit of grace.

Well, let’s hear it TOC, I want to see those suns and clouds in the comments. Before you do though, can we just take a moment to breathe in, smile, give a little laugh that we managed to beat Michigan coming into the game on a 6 game losing streak? Please make sure you irritate every weasel you see this week, especially the Walmart ones, because even with the loaded excuses that are sure to pour out, Paul is still going to be back where he belongs. Go Green!

msu.headline: Instant Recap: Michigan State Takes Down um, 15-6
msu.body:
Nov 7, 2026; Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA; Michigan State Spartans wide receiver Chrishon McCray (13) runs the ball against the Michigan Wolverines at Michigan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rick Osentoski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

From early on in this game, and as many people already knew, it was clear that this was a game between two not good teams.  Unfortunately for us Spartan fans, we have had a couple unlucky breaks while tonight’s opponent has had some good fortune in their season.  Watching the two teams in the first half, one would imagine their records were closer than the reality.

Michigan State got the ball first and moved the chains one time before punting.

On their first defensive stand, Michigan State got a turnover when safety Devin Vaught came down with a pick after a pass went off an um receiver’s finger tips.

Starting a yard inside um territory, the Spartans reached 4th & 2 on the first series.  Coach Fitzgerald decided to be aggressive, and the play call was for a deep shot.  Personally, I would have rather punted here to try pinning an unimpressive offense deep.  Predictably, the deep shot did not pay off.  Receiver Bryson Williams had a chance at it but dropped the pass.

The two teams traded punts on their next possessions, totaling 17 yards of offense between them.  On um’s ensuing drive, they had their best drive of the half, moving 71 yards in 13 plays over six and a half minutes.  They reached the MSU 7, but a 3rd & 1 run lost a yard and brought out the field goal unit.  The kick went off the near side upright and bounced out, keeping the game with no points on the board.

Again, the two teams traded punts.  Getting the ball right at the 50, the Spartans marched all the way to the 3-yard line before having to settle for a field goal, which Liam Boyd made.  Just like that, the Spartans were ahead.

MSU then forced a 3-and-out.  Chrishon McCray muffed the punt reception but retrieved the fumble, and MSU took over at their own 44.  MSU picked up a couple first downs, the second on a 35-yard pass to McCray that got the Spartans down to the 13.  A bogus offensive pass interference penalty in the endzone pushed MSU back near the 20 and eventually led to another FG try, which Boyd comfortably made.

There was only time for a kneel-down after the kickoff, and MSU took a 6-0 lead to the break.  Our defense only gave up 78 total yards through two quarters.

MSU started the second half on defense, and after giving up a first down on the first play, forced a punt.  Unfortunately for us, that punt was allowed to land and it flatlined at the 1-yard line, pinning Alessio Milivojevic and the MSU offense against the goalline.

Starting from the 1-yard line, Michigan State had, perhaps, their most impressive drive since week 2.  The Spartans held the ball for 10:41 of game clock, ran 17 plays, and picked up 6 first downs.  There were passes, runs, wildcats, and overall dominance from MSU.  After reaching the um 12, the offense finally came to a halt with a run for a loss and then a sack.  Liam Boyd came on and hit his 3rd field goal, this one from 38 yards, to put MSU up 9-0.

On um’s ensuing drive, the referees started trying to help the home team.  After it looked like MSU was going to force a 3-and-out, a penalty was called for “illegal substitution” because an MSU defender had the heel of his shoe still on the field when the ball was snapped.  So um got another crack at a 3rd down play, on which MSU was called for pass interference (after a called reception was overturned).  On the next play, um ran the ball through the middle of the Spartan defense, but Lafaele punched the ball out late and Nikai Martinez recovered the loose ball.  Of course, after the play, MSU was penalized 15 yards for celebrating.

After a 28-yard catch-and-run by Chrishon McCray, MSU went backwards for a few plays and ended up punting, but Rhys Dakin pinned um at their own 7 with 12:01 to play.

After giving up a first down to start the drive, the Spartan defense then tackled um for a loss of a yard on a running play, followed that up with a sack by Derrick Simmons, and then got an interception from NiJhay Burt on a deep shot at the MSU 38.

Back on offense, the highlight of the drive was a 36-yard play to Bryson Williams.  The drive lasted 10 plays and over 5 minutes of game clock, and ended in Boyd’s fourth field goal to put MSU up 12-0.

With just over 5 minutes left, um needed to do something quick.  Instead, they held the ball for two plays, fumbling at their 37-yard line after a catch.  NiJhay Burt forced and recovered the fumble.

The Spartans ran the ball three times, then brought Boyd on to hit a 49-yard kick for a 15-0 lead.

The MSU defense then forced a turnover on downs on the first series of um’s possession… but a pass interference gave um an extra life.  After two incompletions and an 11-yard sack, MSU surrendered a 22-yard pass on 4th down.  An 11-yard run moved the chains again for um.  Two plays later, they hit a 31-yard pass to the 1, and then scored a play later to ruin the Spartan shutout.  Now trailing 15-6, um elected to go for two, but Kenny Soares shut that down with an amazing spin move to get home for the sack.

The kickoff was an obvious onside attempt, but the ball only went 6 yards before hitting an um player, giving MSU the ball.  Three kneeldowns later, it was game over and VICTORY FOR MSU!!!!

Sure, it would have been even sweeter to get the shutout, but this was still a dominant win against our rival in a game no one, including myself and many here among TOC Nation, was really giving us much of a chance to win.  For the game, MSU outgained um 298-192 and controlled the clock with over 38 minutes of possession.  The defense created four turnovers.  As Pat Fitzgerald said after the game, “Paul Bunyan is coming home to East Lansing!”

While it can still be said that this was a game between two not good teams, it is clear that um is much more not good than MSU.

tigers.headline: RHP Dustin May may fit the Tigers’ needs for starting pitching depth
tigers.body:
ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 27: Dustin May #21 of the Milwaukee Brewers throws a pitch during the first inning against the Tampa Bay Rays in game four of the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on October 27, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With the near certainty of a lockout and a long fight between players and owners this offseason, it’s hard to get real enthusiastic about free agency right now. It’s usually hard for Tigers’ fans in the first place. While there is the idea being floated that top free agent Tarik Skubal may sign before the December 1st lockout if the right offer is available, with the Dodgers, Mets, and Cubs, generally regarded as his main suitors, he’s a pretty unique case. Apart from Skubal, there seems to be widespread expectation that most free agents will wait until new terms of the next collective bargaining agreement are announced before signing. Likewise, teams need to know the payroll constraints they’ll be working under to really manage their budget for free agents.

However, there’s also likely to be a set of moves from many teams simply designed to shore up depth where possible before the lockout begins. Scott Harris has a habit of trying to add a depth starter early in the offseason. These moves have generally gone pretty poorly, although Drew Anderson was a better choice last year than most. Even so, Harris certainly seems to emphasize getting a little depth in his offseason shopping early on, perhaps with the idea that he won’t have to force a move later. This strategy has not worked out terribly well, but that’s more been a matter of picking the wrong pitchers. The theory is still reasonably sound, particularly with the lockout looming. I wouldn’t be surprised to see him try it again.

The Tigers have a pretty solid group to build a rotation out of next season, but they aren’t necessarily that deep either. By 2028 the Tigers may have a pretty good crop of starting pitching prospects in the upper minors. Right now, they do not. And as we’ve discussed repeatedly since the regular season ended, the Tigers need for high leverage relievers is best answered by converting 1-2 of their starters with big stuff, but limited recent workloads, into relief help. To do that they’re going to need to pick up another starting option this offseason.

The criteria is pretty simple. We’re just looking at short term deals here. The Tigers are highly unlikely to go after a big target in the starting pitching market. National media is going to continue to report that the Tigers are “keeping tabs” on the Tarik Skubal market, but no one is buying that as long as the reported price tag remains well over $300 million. The Tigers will be angling for depth here unless Scott Harris decides to break his usual patterns, so it’s not going to be a thrilling signing when and if they add an arm. Deciding to lock up a decidedly mediocre journeyman reliever in Jacob Waguespack should probably be seen as the corollary to any depth starter signing that could come before the lockout begins.

Let’s take a look at Dustin May, who is a pretty good all around fit for what the Tigers will probably look for in a free agent starter.

RHP Dustin May

SeasonIPERAFIPK%BB%HR/9fWAR2025132.14.964.8821.19.61.430.72026145.24.703.6323.28.10.862.8

This veteran right-hander makes some sense for the Tigers. The lanky 29-year-old has never been able to translate his velocity into high-end whiff rates, and his breaking stuff has never carved hitters up the way many expected when he was a prospect. On the other hand, he’s fairly consistent and took a notable leap in preventing home runs this season while finally putting his years in injury purgatory behind him.

Between 2021-2024, when he was still with the Dodgers, May’s career was in shambles as he had two UCL reconstruction surgeries with just a brief comeback in between them. He was still effective in his brief stints on the mound, but his early potential was going to waste as his mid-20’s were largely spent on the injured list. He was traded to the Boston Red Sox at the deadline in 2025. The Cardinals signed him to a one-year deal worth $12.5M for 2026 before they dealt him to the World Series champs back at the trade deadline. For two seasons now he’s been generally healthy, throwing 132.1 and 145.2 innings the past two seasons, with no major injury trouble.

May is still averaging just shy of 97 mph on his fourseam and sinker with a bit more than average extension. He’s largely backing that with his 93-94 mph cutter in a very fastball heavy profile. He uses his 86 mph sweeper a decent amount, but the break on that is a little too big to fool major league hitters as much as the movement might predict. May rips his 86 mph sweeper at over 3000 rpms, and late in the season, he started throwing more of a straight curveball at 83.7 mph, with the same monstrous spin rate and getting more whiffs with it. We didn’t see it working as effectively in the postseason. In general, May gets a very balanced spread of grounders, line drives, and fly balls, so he’s fairly neutral in terms of how park factors will affect him.

He still feels to me like a guy who might be better off ditching the cutter and trying to throw more of a prototypical slider instead, while continuing to experiment with the sweeper/curveball combo as more of a strike stealer that is hard to square up for lefties. Sometimes throwing cutters, fourseamers, and sinkers all can diminish each of those pitches individually by requiring some fairly subtle feel differences how they’re gripped and released.

However, May was with the Dodgers a long time, so I would guess there have been plenty of stuff experiments under smart coaches along the way. The intriguing note for me was his increased curveball usage late in the year and the velocity on that pitch. Both Jackson Jobe and Beau Brieske started ripping an 85-86 mph curveball that neither had really thrown before, and the pitch looked pretty whiffish in the brief looks we had of them. Possibly the Brewers were thinking along similar lines with May, making this a little more interesting fit in Detroit.

May intrigues me to a degree is that he’s missed a lot of time in his career and really hasn’t had long stretches of good health in which to actually hone his craft and get better. Of course, you can just as easily call that being injury prone, but you take a look at May’s raw stuff and the wildly varying arm angles from year to year, it feels like he’s still tinkering for the right arm angle and stuff.

The Tigers don’t really need a workhorse here. May just completed back-to-back full seasons for the first time in his major league career, and yet he’s been with four teams over those two seasons. He hasn’t had a chance to settle in anywhere. And yet, May had a pretty good first half before fading as the season progressed. His 4.38 ERA with the Cardinals was solid, and he boasted a 3.15 FIP in St. Louis that said he’d actually been somewhat unlucky. He dealt with back tightness in June and then an ankle contusion in July, and really wasn’t pitching well through that stretch.

May briefly got off to a good start in Milwaukee, but blew up in a start on August 19th and the next time out took a 106 mph liner to his back, striking him in the upper back on the right side. He struggled the rest of the way, posting an ERA of 5.65 with the Brewers as they limited his starts and kept a quick hook on him. He was okay in the postseason, but again was working short outings with a mix of starts and relief appearances after an opener.

May dominates right-handed hitters. His trouble has always been allowing power and walks to lefties. In 2026, the problem was really just those walks. The Tigers being in pretty good shape with lefty relievers says that May would have a quick hook hanging over him in the middle innings of any start where a tough pocket of lefties was coming up in the opposing lineup.

Things are set up pretty well for May to have a solid season in 2027. I wouldn’t expect much more than 125-145 innings, but his production should be basically league average or a little better. He would be the Tigers’ fifth starter, and might get flexed into middle relief work here and there as well. That would allow the Tigers to use one of River Ryan, Troy Melton, or Keider Montero in high leverage roles along with Drew Sommers and hopefully, Will Vest next year. If Reese Olson is finally healthy, that opens up more options.

I’m not convinced that May has tons of upside remaining or anything, but his velocity and ability to spin the baseball will continue to intrigue teams around the league. The Tigers would be happy with his Cardinals production during most of the 2026 season, and hope to help him be more consistent from start to start and cut down on the walks to lefties. Solid depth starter work with some flexibility would do just fine, though he’ll likely be angling for a two-year deal after proving that he’s finally beyond all the elbow troubles.

MLB Trade Rumors projects a two-year, $30M deal with a player opt-out after year one. Like most contracts of this type, you’re rarely going to love it, but it might be just what the Tigers need to allow them to focus on the bullpen.

You all have mastered the art of commenting but can you name a former baseball player faster than your fellow commenters? tigers.headline: Tigers announce 2027 coaching and training staff
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 17: Manager A.J. Hinch #14 of the Detroit Tigers looks on against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on September 17, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Tigers confirmed recent reports on hirings for their 2027 coaching staff on Friday. They announced the hiring of Kyle Hudson as the new first base and baserunning coach. Hudson worked with outfielders in his most recent job as Boston Red Sox’s third base coach, so perhaps he’ll take on some of those responsibilities in Detroit as well. Still the emphasis from the Tigers is on the baserunning side. Hudson was also an assistant coach for the Cleveland Guardians from 2020-2022 before joining the Red Sox.

The Tigers had already hired longtime major league catcher Martin Maldonado, whom AJ Hinch worked with briefly in Houston, as their new quality coach this offseason. Maldonado was behind the plate during the Astros 2022 run to the World Series championship. He brings a strong reputation as a leader and game planner, as well as his skill coaching the position, to the Tigers.

Longtime catching coach Ryan Sienko, who joined the organization in 2021, AJ Hinch’s first year as manager, will retain his duties coaching catchers, but will also now handle duties as bullpen coach following Juan Nieves departure from the organization. It’s typically a pitching coach in that role, so that’s a bit interesting. Presumably, Maldonado will handle more of the pre-game pitch planning with Dillon Dingler and Eduardo Valencia, while Sienko will continue coaching the actual catching skills, but perhaps their responsibilities will be mixed between them as well.

The Tigers have yet to replace Gabe Ribas as director of pitching in the farm system after his departure to work for the Colorado Rockies last offseason. They’ve replaced Nieves, who has been Chris Fetter’s assistant pitching coach since 2021, with a catcher, leaving Fetter and assistant Robin Lund as a duo to coach the pitchers. Perhaps they’ll end up hiring a new pitching director this offseason, but it’s a bit peculiar that they’re cutting out both major and minor league pitching coaches. Those responsibilities still have to be fulfilled by someone, but without some detailed clarification from the organization it’s difficult to pin down who is actually doing what at this point in regard to those roles.

The Tigers have named Kyle Hudson as their major league first base and baserunning coach.

Martin Maldonado has been named major league quality coach.

Hudson and Maldonado join manager A.J. Hinch’s coaching staff that otherwise returns intact from the end of the 2026 campaign,…
— Tigers PR (@DetroitTigersPR) November 6, 2026

George Lombard is expected to stay on for his seventh year as Tigers bench coach under Hinch. Billy Boyer took over from Joey Cora as third base coach during the 2026 season and seems set to remain in that role. Beyond Maldonado, Hudson, Sienko, Fetter, and Lund, the Tigers are working with a three-man group of hitting coaches. Michael Brdar, Cody Asche, and Lance Zawadski, who seem set to be retained for 2027. Boyer was the Tigers quality control coach last season, and will cede that job to Maldonado.

Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic also reports that the Tigers have hired Scott Peters as their new medical director, while Jeremiah Randle has been hired as the Tigers new athletic trainer. Peters was most recently the director of health and performance science for the Toronto Blue Jays. Randall was the head athletic trainer for the Astros from 2016-2025.

Former head trainer Ryan Eubanks and assistent trainer Chris McDonald parted ways with the Tigers organization at season’s end.

The Tigers also confirmed the hiring of Jay Sartori as Vice President of Baseball Operations. Sartori was formerly an assistant general manager in the organization going back to the beginning of the Tigers rebuild in 2017. He left last season for a college job in the ACC but has returned to the fold this offseason.

tigers.headline: Beau Ankeney mashed his way onto the prospect radar in 2026
tigers.body:
PHOENIX, AZ - MARCH 29: Beau Ankeney (35) Grand Canyon Infielder takes a big swing during a baseball game between the Arizona Wildcats and the Grand Canyon Lopes on March 29, 2022, at GCU Ballpark in Phoenix, AZ. (Photo by Zac BonDurant/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

There are two particular categories of player that go under the radar in the major league amateur draft each year. The first are college seniors. If you didn’t get drafted by your junior year or earlier, as a JUCO or prep player, there’s a natural stigma attached. The second are first basemen. Because the position is usually filled by less athletic players whose value is heavily tied up in their bat, only the top ranked college first baseman really get much notice, and they tend to go in the early rounds as some of the better hitters each year. Leaving aside the player and just considering the profile, Spencer Torkelson was a hard player to philosophically wrap one’s head around as the first overall pick in the draft back in 2020. Living up to that would’ve required him to develop quickly into one of the better hitters in baseball. There’s a reason you very rarely see a 1-1 first baseman.

Detroit Tigers prospect Beau Ankeney checks both boxes, and he definitely didn’t get much attention on draft day 2025 when they picked him in the 14th round out of Loyola Marymount and paid him just the minimum signing bonus. He played three years at Grand Canyon University before breaking out and transferring to Loyola for his senior season in 2025. That was notable, as he was clearly a bit of a late bloomer. Also notable was his muscular six-foot-three, 235 pound frame. He only played in four games after the draft, so there wasn’t anything to get excited about yet. That changed in 2026.

Ankeney mashed 24 home runs total, including 9 in just 27 games at the High-A level after he was promoted in late July. He took his walks. He showed pretty good athleticism for a first baseman, with enough speed to handle a corner outfield spot here and there. His raw power really stood out, as he averaged 92 mph off the bat, which is great even at the MLB level, and maxed out at 114.4 mph off the bat, giving him a 65 FV grade on his raw power potential. And most importantly, he took his walks and didn’t strike out that much for a power hitter.

In Lakeland at Single-A, Ankeney chased about 30 percent of the time, and his whiff rate was similarly on the higher end of the scale. Considering that he was 23 years old already and competing with 19-22 year old players quite a bit, it was impressive, but didn’t really knock anyone’s socks off. What really got prospect hounds talking was the fact that he went straight into High-A and did even more damage, without much of an increase in his strikeout rate. From August 4 through the 16th, Ankeney hit seven homers in nine games while walking and racking up one multi-hit game after another. He was the hottest hitter in the league for that stretch before cooling down over the final weeks of the season.

Beau Ankeney is on an all-time heater. He crushes another homer here to put the Whitecaps up 5-3. It’s his 2nd of the game, his 5th in his last 5 games, and his 7th in 14 games at High-A. Sheesh. @ThatDanHasty calls it. pic.twitter.com/TK36VMUrD6
— Tigers ML Report (@tigersMLreport) August 15, 2026

He does chase too much right now, and there’s some swing and miss in his game, producing at 24.3 percent K-rate in Single-A, and 27.5 percent in High-A, but that’s not terrible either. He also showed nice feel at times for hitting the ball where it’s pitched, driving fastballs away to right field with authority, and hitting tape measure shots to center and left-center when he got something middle or middle-in over the plate. He hits from an upright stance and is pretty flat through the hitting zone, making him strong against the high fastball. He can get some tilt to launch sinkers and secondary pitches that hang up in the zone as well, but a pitcher that pounds the bottom rail can give him trouble. Still, it’s a compact inside-out move that works to the big part of the field pretty well as long as he doesn’t get too pull happy. He struggled some with breaking stuff and that will be something to watch as the pitching he’s facing gets tougher, but he hit for average and plenty of power against fastballs and offspeed stuff.

Obviously there’s a caveat here due to his age. He’s a little older and more physically mature than a lot of the pitchers he faced this season. The short sample in the Midwest League to close out the season was really impressive though, and lends credence to the idea that he was putting it together nicely late in his first pro season. Another plus for him is the athleticism, in that he isn’t the typical big hitting statue you typically find in a college first baseman.

I’m not going to get too carried away just yet, but it’s good to see another power-hitting right-handed bat with potential in the system. Hopefully we’ll see him refine his approach and start to handle the nastier stuff he’s seeing at the High-A level more consistently next season. He’s probably never going to be a high contact hitter and there’s certainly risk in the hit tool, but the fact that he sprays the ball around is pretty promising for his future batting average projections. So is the batspeed and hard contact he’s mustering.

Beau Ankeney wasn’t the biggest breakout prospect of the year for the Tigers, but he was among the least expected and should feel great about his full season debut. No doubt the Tigers do.

tigers.headline: Detroit Tigers 2026 BYB preseason prospect list review #21-30
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers catcher Eduardo Valencia (32) is interviewed after helping bring in the win against the Pittsburgh Pirates at Comerica Park in Detroit on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

This is installment three of our look back at the 2026 BYB preseason prospect rankings and scouting reports for the Detroit Tigers. Typically, we don’t revisit each prospect on our rankings until we re-grade them for next year’s reports and rankings in the leadup to spring training. This year, with a potentially much longer offseason while the CBA negotiations go one, we thought we’d revisit the full rankings and just give a quick assessment of the year went for each player, what improvements they made, or still need to make, and whether their prospect stock is trending up, down, or neutral as the offseason begins.

Most of the players in this ground from the 21st spot to the 30th spot are 40+ FV prospects. Izaac Pacheco, at 30, is the only one from the 40 FV tier in this article. You can find the full prospect list, with links to each individual scouting report right here. Once again, this is just a look back at the preseason grades and rankings, so players added during the season either in trade or via the draft, aren’t included.

21- RHP Dylan Smith

One of the more surprising DFA decisions of the Tigers season came right as they set their Opening Day roster and decided to put this 25-year-old right-handed reliever on waivers, ultimately trading him to the Giants for cash considerations. Smith went on to throw 39.2 innings for the Giants, collecting four saves while blowing five, with a 3.86 ERA and a 3.63 FIP on the year, good for 0.5 fWAR. That’s about as much as they could’ve hoped for when they dealt for Smith. He doesn’t have closer caliber stuff, and wouldn’t crack the setup man level for many teams.

We’re not going to lose a ton of sleep over a middle reliever with modest ability to handle a setup role, but right-handers like that were in rather short supply for the Tigers at multiple points during the 2026 season. Just a strange bit of roster mismanagement perhaps indicating some overconfidence in their bullpen depth back in March. Smith’s fourseam-slider combination was effective enough for a solid strikeout rate with the Giants and he limited home runs, but some of that is probably related to Oracle Park being a difficult place to hit homers, as Smith allowed a much higher fly ball percentage than he did in the minors. There may have been an element of pitching to the park as well. He still needs to command both pitches more consistently and limit walks to move into regular high leverage setup work, but he took a pretty nice step in his first full year in the major leagues.

Stock: Neutral

22- RHP Ty Madden

Ty Madden spent years in the Tigers system trying to overcome a fourseam fastball with mediocre shape and declining velocity. His command developed pretty nicely considering the deep pitch mix he wields, but some of his issues have never been fully worked out. The club’s competitive balance pick in Round A back in 2021, much was expected of Madden at the time, and very little has been produced. He made a short debut in 2024 and then missed the 2025 season with a rotator cuff injury. Heading into his age 26 season, we still held out hope that Madden would provide some value in relief.

His pre-injury velocity did not fully come back, but Madden thrived pretty well anyway, utilizing his deep pitch mix more effectively in 2026. It took him some time to get on track at Triple-A, but he eventually started finding his groove and eventually threw 46 innings of middle relief for the Tigers with a 3.26 ERA and a 3.55 FIP combination. Putting a 40+ grade on him was a bit ambitious coming back from major shoulder issues, but Madden lived up to the billing. He knows how to pitch and has learned to mix fourseamers, sinkers, and cutters to take pressure off the fourseamer. With a good slider and a decent splitter and knuckle curve, Madden has the arsenal of a starter, but the pitchability of a potentially valuable middle reliever who can handle going through an order multiple times.

I’m not sure there’s much left to squeeze out of his game at this point. The high 90’s velocity he had as a premier college starter has faded a bit, and unless some radical development occurs, this is probably pretty close to his level. The Tigers have been trying to build more ride into the fourseamer for years, and despite a little higher arm slot this year it’s still pretty mediocre action on it. Still, as the first year after a pretty major injury, it was a success. If Madden can get back to his old consistency with his breaking stuff and punch out more hitters nex year, he’ll be even better equipped to handle a mix of longer relief work along with some setup opportunities. It’s just a pretty similar profile to Drew Anderson’s likely position in the bullpen.

Stock: Neutral

23. RHP Michael Massey

Wake Forest alum Michael Massey might be the best pure relief arm in the Tigers’ system. They drafted him in the 4th round of the 2024 draft, and then watched him follow so many of the Tigers top pitchers drafted onto the injury list in his first year of pro ball. After missing all that time for Tommy John surgery and rehab, all we really wanted this year was to see him back on the mound. We got that much as Massey made two short starts late in the year.

Happily, the stuff is still really good. Massey was steadily 94-95 mph with over seven feet of extension to the plate. His most notable quality is the enormous riding action on that fastball due to his high arm slot and release, and that returned intact as well. He averaged nearly 20 inches of induced vertical break, and while we’d love to see him build up to 97-98 mph over the next year or two, the movement and extension makes this a plus fastball already with good potential for more.

The six-foot-five, 230 pounder has the frame to keep building velocity into his mid-20’s. His curveball is another plus pitch, pairing really well with the heater out of Massey’s high arm slot. He packs a pretty good slider as well. Now the challenge is to stay healthy in 2027, build up his arm, and get on with refining his command. That high arm slot requires him to clear his head off the target line a little early, and timing that up can be tricky, but he has the athleticism to make it work. Massey should move very quickly as long as the Tigers develop him as a reliever as expected.

Until we see him settle in for a full season and improve his strike-throwing, we’ll hold him with a 40+ grade, but he has really high end potential in the bullpen. If the velocity and command develop as projected, Massey could be a closing option for the Tigers down the road. The only goal in 2026 was just to get back on the mound. We’ll see where things go from there.

Stock: Neutral

24- C/1B Eduardo Valencia

We were very impressed with Valencia’s breakout at the plate in 2025, but it was still hard to envision a regular role for him with the Tigers, limiting his upside. A decidedly bat first player with a good approach, letting fastballs travel and taking them the opposite way while turning on and crushing breaking balls and changeups, there was a lot to like coming into 2026, and Valencia proved the breakout was real with a really nice major league debut. He hit 8 homers in 42 games while batting .341 and coming up with plenty of big knocks along the way. There was plenty of good fortune on balls in play, and I don’t think Valencia is going to be a consistent .300 hitter, but he is dangerous and kept the strikeouts in check fairly well. If he can be a little more selective in his swing decisions, he should remain a very productive hitter.

The really interesting part of his season was the improvements behind the plate. I still don’t love him as a second catcher, as teams are running more and Valencia’s arm is pretty stretched behind the plate. On the other hand, his framing, blocking, and game calling were all improved to roughly average levels after an impressive offseason’s work. Coming into the season I thought we might have just have a pinch-hitting specialist who could possibly improve as a first baseman but wouldn’t end up catching that much. Instead, Valencia turned himself into a more viable backup to Dillon Dingler and also showed leadership ability and a knack for the big moment. His teammates really seemed to rally around him at times.

Those defensive improvements really help the profile, and bump him up a full grade as he graduates from the system. Valencia is not really built to be an everyday player, but as a backup catcher who will get a lot of plate appearances in the DH slot, he’s got a regular role carved out for himself next year.

Stock: Up

25- RHP Rayner Castillo

This 22-year-old sinkerballer made a fairly impressive full season debut in Single-A back in 2024, but hasn’t been able to take the next steps to break into the upper minors. That’s not surprising considering his age, but now we have back-to-back years with only minor progress. Castillo has a smooth, easy delivery that was steadily producing a tough mid-90’s sinker in 2024 and 2025, but the secondary pitches were still behind the curve. He had a tough go again for parts of this season, but eventually the slider started rounding into form. Just as the strikeouts started to pile up late in the year, he was knocked out in a rough start on September 1 and was shut down at 87.1 innings.

Castillo projected as a future depth starter with possible mid-rotation upside due to his youth and raw stuff. His slider improved this year, but his command of the slider and changeup was still pretty spotty. Still, it’s the glimpses of easy mid-90’s velocity, nasty sink, and high ground ball rate that make him a name worth watching. The fastball command should continue to improve, and he’s still young enough to be optimistic about his secondary pitches becoming more trustworthy weapons. The Tigers may have a pretty good starting pitcher here in time. So, we’ll hold him around this level with a 40+ grade and see if he can put it together and conquer High-A in 2027.

Stock: Neutral

26- OF Brett Callahan

We were higher on Callahan than most in 2024-2025 as he battled a litany of small injuries. Heading into 2026, he finally got some national love and some overcompensated for being late on him by getting a bit too excited. He did reward our confidence in his all around game with a strong campaign at Double-A Erie before leaping quickly through Triple-A to reach the major leagues. Unfortunately, his free swinging ways continued and Callahan got himself out a lot by chasing. As a result, he didn’t tap into his above average raw power much at all after hitting 12 homers in 60 games at Double-A in the first half.

Callahan is a well rounded player, but whether he can lay off chase pitches enough to contribute offensively remains an open question. His rapid trajectory to the majors this year certainly pressed the issue, but he made no progress in his swing decisions. The leap in pitching was just too much for him as he put up a chase rate of 40.1 percent and didn’t make much hard contact. That isn’t sustainable at the big league level, but he didn’t get much time to acclimate himself either. My sense is that Callahan was a little overwhelmed by the rapid promotions and just never settled in after leaving Erie.

The now 25-year-old needs to adapt and improve his approach significantly to get better pitches to hit. If he does, he should do enough damage to earn regular playing time, as the rest of his game is pretty solid, but it’s just a depth outfielder profile unless he can take that big step in 2027. Expect Callahan to work out of Toledo next season while the Tigers see what they have left in Kerry Carpenter and Parker Meadows. That will give him time to work on his approach, and opportunities to get back to the majors will be his for the taking if he can improve.

Stock: Neutral

27- OF Jackson Strong

Another small college outfielder like Callahan, the 23-year-old Strong is developing into a good center fielder, but there are plenty of issues with the hit tool as well. He has some pop and good speed, and does a decent job controlling the strike zone and taking his walks. He hit 17 homers and stole 22 bases for the High-A West Michigan Whitecaps this season while walking a whopping 15.6 percent of the time and playing a pretty nice center field. Unfortunately, he also swings and misses a lot even in the zone, and that was the issue we were looking for improvement with this season. Instead, he struck out nearly 30 percent of the time.

Strong is still working with a fairly grooved swing. He’s a low ball hitter who struggles to cover the upper half of the zone, and is often caught chasing breaking balls and changeups as he hunts for pitches down in the zone. He does show flashes of above average power, but getting to more of it as he progresses is going to be difficult with a lot of chase and too many whiffs as well. The learning curve is steeper for small college hitters who didn’t see much high level stuff, which was part of the pitch for patience with Strong last year. Even so, there aren’t too many hitters who break through and become major league regulars after punching out this much in A-ball.

His speed and defensive ability certainly give him a clean path to an eventual big league role, but the bat has a lot of catching up to do to carry him that far. We gave Strong some benefit of the doubt last spring, and it just didn’t come together. He’s still young enough to wait on, but it got harder to buy into Strong’s bat this year. Even so, legit center fielders with power don’t grow on trees, so the Tigers will have plenty of patience with him.

Stock: Down

28- RHP Moises Rodriguez

This 24-year-old right-hander has a nasty sinker that sometimes touches triple digits. One of the few really interesting pure relief prospects in the system, Rodriguez entered the season at Double-A in need of better command of both the sinker and his slider and unfortunately didn’t make any real progress. He still racked up a massive ground ball rate just shy of 59 percent and rarely allows any home runs, but it remains a difficult profile to float without better command of the sinker. I’d like to see him add some muscle and improve his lower half stability this offseason and hopefully become more consistent in spotting it to both sides of the plate. He’s still an interesting relief option who could develop into something like prime Jason Foley, but while he posted a 2.57 ERA in making the jump to Double-A, there just aren’t enough whiffs in the profile to project much of a major league career if can’t make that happen.

Stock: Down

29- CF Seth Stephenson

After finally conquering High-A with a 2025 season that saw Stephenson make notable improvements in his batspeed and tap into more power, it looked like his contact and speed game had finally gotten the needed boost. Instead, Stephenson struck out more in his first full season at the Double-A level and the power dried up completely. He missed a little time to injury in May, tore it up in June upon his return, but then really faded again in July and August. He did steal 66 bases, illustrating the traits that keep him an interesting young player at a point where the game seems to be valuing speed and contact more highly again. The Eastern League limited pickoff throws to just one this year, and Stephenson and teammate Peyton Graham took full advantage.

There’s still a chance for a Chandler Simpson type player who sprays the ball around and uses his feet to help him hit for average. The problem is that after doing a lot better job of it at the High-A level last year, Stephenson stopped catching balls solidly out in front of the plate and was back in slap and dash mode for most of the year. Most of his fly balls were either pop-ups or routine flyouts where he’s a little late. Getting to even decent gap power looks less likely now, and while his top shelf speed makes him an above average center fielder, Stephenson’s route running and closing ability remain rough around the edges. There’s a role for this type of player but only if he can start driving better pitching more often next year. He’ll be 26 in January, so further progress needs to come quickly.

Stock: Down

30- 3B/1B Izaac Pacheco

Pacheco was the one player in this group with a 40 grade last offseason. After four straight years trying to break out of the High-A level, the slugging third baseman finally managed a much improved season in 2025 and got himself back on the radar to a degree. Unfortunately, all the same issues reared their heads at the Double-A level. His power potential remains enormous, and he did a little better job getting to it this season, hitting 24 home runs, 21 of them at the Double-A level. On the other hand, better pitching carved him up routinely as Pacheco posted a brutal 33.9 percent strikeout rate. After years of adjustments and swing changes, he’s tapping into his power at the bottom of the zone but still struggles to cover the rest of the plate with any real consistency even against fastballs. There are just so many comfortable ways for better pitchers to get him out while avoiding Pacheco’s sweet spots in the strike zone.

One saving grace is that his defense at the corners is actually pretty solid. He’s more than a future possible DH. There’s still a pathway to the major leagues for Pacheco, but it remains very narrow. He’s refined his swing and approach to hit a lot of fly balls to the pull field specifically because he has to maximize the damage on his limited amounts of hard contact. To carry that approach to the majors, he’s got to become more selective in his swing decisions. This three true outcomes type of hitting profile is rapidly disappearing around the game, and only players with a great eye for doing damage, like Munetaka Murakami, are really making it work. Pacheco will turn 24 in two weeks, so he really needs to make some adjustments and conquer upper level pitching next season or he’ll be left behind as the next waves of Tigers prospects pass him by.

Stock: Down

tigers.headline: Tigers decline option on RHP Kenley Jansen, exercise option on RHP Drew Anderson
tigers.body:
DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 22: Drew Anderson #38 of the Detroit Tigers pitches against the Washington Nationals during the third inning at Comerica Park on September 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Duane Burleson/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Today is the deadline for option decisions, as well as for reinstating players off the 60-day injured list. The Tigers just released their flurry of moves, most notably exercising their $10 million club option for 2027 on RHP Drew Anderson, and declining their 2027 option on RHP Kenley Jansen. They’ll pay the veteran closer, just two saves shy of becoming the third closer in MLB history to reach 500 for his career, two million to buy out the $12 million club option. In addition, they made a surprise move, signing RHP Jacob Waguespack to a one-year, $1.3 million guaranteed deal for 2027. Waguespack’s contract comes with an extra $200K in potential bonuses he can earn next season.

Probably the most surprising part of the Tigers decisions today was the fact that they reinstated seven of eight players from the 60-day injured list. The only player they didn’t reinstate was left-hander Bailey Horn, who had Tommy John surgery during the season and is expected to miss all of the 2027 season. He was placed on unconditional release waivers along with RHP Sawyer Gipson-Long.

The Tigers did reinstate OF Kerry Carpenter, OF Parker Meadows, OF Wenceel Perez, OF Matt Vierling, RHP Reese Olson, RHP Will Vest, and INF Trey Sweeney. OF Corey Julks was outrighted and is now a free agent, while RHP Yilber Diaz was designated for assignment.

Some of the players they kept still aren’t going to make it through the offseason, as the Tigers 40-man roster now stands full at 40 players. Keeping Carpenter, Meadows, Vest, and Olson were obvious moves, but hanging onto Matt Vierling yet again doesn’t appeal to me at all. Sweeney and Perez don’t really have much path to a future role either. And of course we have no real updates on any of their medical conditions.

The Tigers still have to add prospects Josue Briceño and Max Anderson to the 40-man soon, and so two more players will have to come off the 40-man to make that happen. And of course any free agent signings or claims of players who have to go on the 40-man will require a corresponding move to open a spot.

One real surprise here to me is Waguespack. He was certainly effective for the Tigers, putting up a 2.49 ERA, but the 32-year-old just doesn’t get many whiffs and isn’t notably good at limiting hard contact either. Yilber Diaz is still wild but has a lot hotter stuff and is six years younger.

Still, this is only temporary housekeeping, and further moves will alter the 40-man roster anyway. Waguespack is a little cheap insurance for now, until we see if there are major moves in free agency or whether everyone is largely waiting for the lockout. It still seems fairly likely that the Tigers will try to pursue a one-year deal with another starting pitcher for depth before the December 1 lockout. They’ve gone after a cheap depth starter early in the offseason with some regularity in the Scott Harris years.
